en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* (Treatise on the Differentiation of the Sectarian Tenets).

This *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra, refers to "tenets" (*samaya*) as the principles revered by the various sects, and "wheel" (*cakra*) as the function of manifesting the power to crush [opposition].
It is likened to the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) possessed by a king, which is able to... [subdue all enemies].
It is not that he sought to drive away invaders or exterminate enemies. Alas! This *Arhat* of the Bhadrakalpa—how could he be merely one who studies the Hīnayāna?
He also took pity on this degenerate age, wherein people engage in sectarian strife, thereby causing the profound carriage of the Mahāyāna to be stranded upon divergent paths.
Our Great Master Ci'en composed a commentary for this very purpose; it is surely for this reason that this book may be so described.
It is also a marker for the path. Alas! In recent times, the Dharma has declined along with the world;
even those who grease the axles of the Mahāyāna take a narrow road. They jolt along broken slopes, stumbling and faltering, as if they had lost their linchpins and crossbars.
Who knows this? To speak of the mind-nature as inherently pure with such earnestness is entirely identical to the Mahāsāṃghika school;

to chatter incessantly about dependent origination and provisional existence is still confused with the Prajñaptivāda school. What else could this be but a failure to grasp the correct standard? One must not fail to be cautious.
Furthermore, the current version of the *Xingxiang shu* contains many misplaced passages, which may cause difficulties for readers (as noted by Jì). Never before has this been so.

While residing in Nanjing, I obtained one fascicle of this excellent text. I cherished it, storing it away with great care and multiple layers of wrapping. Recently, there have been those who promote its wide circulation;

their resolve is set upon the endurance of the Dharma, and they urge me to hasten its publication in this world. Their exhortations were earnest and repeated, more so than even the exchange of a city for a gem (as in the story of *Ji Bian*).
Since I have always harbored the intention to propagate the Dharma, why should I vainly seek out a good merchant? Thus, I have appended this to the woodblocks, hoping that—

If those of later generations can avoid neglecting this, they will ultimately be illuminated by its radiance, and likewise avoid the error of attempting to practice the Mahāyāna on narrow ground. Thus it is said.
In the first month of spring in the ninth year of the Meirei era, the year of Renchen.
Preface to the *Commentary on the Exposition of the Doctrinal Differences of the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (or *Saṃghabhedavastu*), composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Jibian,
a monk who studied abroad in Nanjing and transmitted the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school.
Although the Eye of the World was extinguished after the Tathāgata entered Nirvāṇa, Kāśyapa, Madhyantika, and others continued to transmit and uphold the Dharma-piṭaka.
The subtle words [of the Buddha] still survive; after more than one hundred years had passed, the learning of Kuṭadanta found no one to inherit it.
Then, the debates of Mahādeva caused the true exegesis to become confused and distorted, and the vying for partisan factions first arose, resulting in two schools:
namely, the Mahāsāṃghika and the Sthavira. From this point onward, the Sthaviras split into eleven schools and the Mahāsāṃghikas divided into nine schools.
Thus, being entangled by the net of views, those who study are dazed and confused, lacking any coherent thread; they weep as they stand at a fork in the great road.
Four hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing], the Great Bodhisattva Vasumitra emerged, fiercely kindling the torch of wisdom to serve as a bright lamp for the world.

Furthermore, he lamented that the monastic community had become decadent and frivolous, with each person asserting "this is right" while denouncing "that is wrong," rising up like swarming bees and splitting apart like mountain streams. For these reasons, he composed this treatise.
This work clarifies the ultimate aim of resolving disputes; furthermore, it is transmitted as the source for the land of Zhina (China).

Chen Zhen Di was the first to translate [the text] and compose commentaries, while the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty corrected the earlier translations and produced a new version. Master Ji compiled this as the *Shuji* (Commentary), excising what the ancient masters had not fully understood.
He eliminated the redundant prose of the old commentaries, pruning and refining them until they were concise; this is truly a great achievement. How could it be otherwise?

Is it not merely that reading these minor treatises provides some benefit? Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are those who have refuted and expelled the tenets of various schools, extracting and summarizing one or two points;
yet, without consulting these established texts, how could one possibly know their origins and conclusions?
Consequently, I have added Japanese annotations to this work and published it for longevity, hoping to disseminate it far and wide so that those who love antiquity might consider examining it.
This parable of the staff and the robe is like selecting genuine gold from the sand.
Written on a fortunate day in the second month of summer in the ninth year of the Genroku era (the *biji* year), by the bhikṣu Chōyu Shikyō,
resident abbot of Ryūhō-ji in Sendai, Ōshū, while dwelling at the foot of Mount Chishaku in Higashiyama, Kyoto.
*Commentary on the Treatise on the Doctrinal Differences of the Various Schools*,
composed by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Recorded by the Sramana Yi, who translated the scriptures:

The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* (Treatise on the Wheel of the Doctrinal Divisions) was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra of the Sarvāstivāda school approximately four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Beholding that the Way was perfected and the capacity for enlightenment awakened, the jade-like radiance thus soared forth.
When his transformative influence had exhausted its karmic conditions and his golden body withdrew its shadow,
although the myriad beings lost their guide under the four rulers and the True Teaching declined in the Five Indias, the Sublime Sages continued to propagate it with a shared understanding. Thus,
from the time after the Twin Trees until a century prior [to the present], there was no report of human contention, nor were there confused doctrines regarding the Dharma.

All this stems from Kāśyapa and Ānanda attending closely upon Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; within, there were five hundred arhats, and without, more than ten thousand who had attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
They were profoundly learned in the purport of the Tripiṭaka and convened at the Seven-Leaf Rock. Although the teachings were propagated in two locations, their realization remained unified.
Now that these holy ones have ceased their transformative activity and returned to the Truth, even the palm-leaf manuscripts [have vanished].
The transmission of the Way remained unbroken until, subsequently, the Venerable Yaśas—the disciple of Ānanda—summoned seven hundred Arhats once more to the country of Vaiśālī for a second council.
There they subdued those who were perverse and reorganized what had become obscure, erroneous, and degenerate.

Although the Dharma flourished during the time of the Pure Elder [Kāśyapa], as the ages shifted, understanding became obscured; the sages grew few while the commoners multiplied, and Mahādeva soon gained the upper hand.

In their debates and rivalries, even the multitude of sages have deeply stirred their emotions and vied with one another; human beings have split into different schools, and the Dharma has diverged into distinct sects.
Like waves churning the profound source or stars scattered across the jeweled peaks, they have caused the single flavor of the subtle teaching to divide into twenty schools.

From this point on, the path of wisdom has become uneven, and it is difficult to choose between the traces of the Way. Although they may be distinguished like white woolen cloth and fine hair, [the underlying truth remains the same].
Having shattered the golden seal and departed from the formal rites, one violates the original intent; harboring biased considerations, one’s emotions stagnate in deviant wisdom.

The Sage possesses universal regulations, yet his physical form conforms to different schools. The Bodhisattva, following conditions to benefit beings through various manifestations, shines forth like a reflection appearing in flowing water—truly a *Arhat* of the Bhadrakalpa who succeeds the Compassionate Honored One as the one to fill his place. Once the cause is perfected and virtue is fulfilled, the fruit awaits.

Spontaneously the Way was perfected; his elaborate thoughts were exquisite and imbued with inner brilliance. His profound sentiments were deep and outstanding, penetrating and encompassing secret springs.
He recounted the origins of the traces to nurture future generations, and his discernment reached the subtle and the minute.

His discourse differed from other schools yet served as a ford for later sages—truly a celestial mirror among the twenty [patriarchs] and a vast source for the various divisions. Formerly, during the Chen dynasty in the region south of the Yangtze River, three...
The Tibetan scholars, relying on their own translation of this work—the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*—have examined it against various palm-leaf manuscripts.
They found that in some instances the terminology deviated from the Sanskrit text, and in others the meaning was inconsistent with the original sense.
Where they had gained insight, they expanded upon it; where they were confused, they excised portions. Now, my personal preceptor, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuan...

On the fourteenth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Longshuo era of the Great Tang, Xuanzang, while serving as a member of the translation bureau at the Qingfu Hall of the Yuhua Palace, retranslated this text.
Having joined the ranks of the translation assistants by virtue of his humble merit, he received imperial instructions to compile a *Shuji* (Commentary) as the work was being translated.
Following the Master’s own sub-commentary (*shu*), he produced ten fascicles, providing a detailed and comprehensive exposition of the various matters and meanings.
Scholars may fear its voluminous text and thus neglect its broad scope; therefore, I shall here clarify its general principles and explain its original text.
Where it differs significantly from previous versions, I will discuss both the major and minor points; where it accords with previous versions, I shall briefly present the essential outline.
The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* (Treatise on the Differentiation of the Doctrinal Schools) raises the grand framework to signal and proclaim the general name of one school;

furthermore, it is called a "treatise" (*śāstra*) to provide an elegant mirror for its title, distinguishing it as a specific designation within the Tripiṭaka. When people follow divergent paths, they are termed "different schools" (*nikāya-bheda*);
when the Dharma deviates from uniformity, it is thus called the "Wheel of Doctrines" (*samaya-cakra*). "Different" (*bhinna*) means distinct; "school" (*nikāya*) means a category.
Furthermore, because people’s understandings and emotional views differ according to their individual capacities, they are categorized into distinct groups; these are called "sects" (*nikāya*).

"Sect" (*zong*) refers to the master or leader, while "wheel" (*lun*) refers to turning. Because the doctrines held by these masters involve mutual acceptance and rejection—much like a wheel that does not remain fixed—it is called the *Zhenglun* (Wheel of Doctrines).
Alternatively, "sect" refers to the principle being venerated, and "wheel" refers to the function of crushing [oppositions], just as a king [uses his wheel].

There is the Wheel-Treasure (cakraratna), which by extinguishing bandits and eliminating enmity establishes great achievements and success; it manifests ability and exalts virtue, serving as a mirror for those who come from afar to study.

Those of various schools who thoroughly master the profound and subtle, and who are exquisitely proficient in the recondite and mysterious, can thus suppress heterodox paths and restrain divergent sects.
Because they plant virtue and spread their fame, they borrow the name of the "Wheel. This treatise on the Wheel-Sectarian School (Cakravāda) is based on the interpretations of the Master Shi.
Furthermore, he vigorously elucidated the ultimate essence of the school, refining his arguments to establish a model for future generations; thus, he titled this work a "Treatise" (*śāstra*).
More than a hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various heterodox schools arose within the holy teachings, which led to what was not beneficial.
The commentary states: The models for composing various treatises differ; however, this present treatise consists of two major sections.

First, it sets forth the intent of its composition, which corresponds to the "causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching. Second, it presents what is elucidated therein, which constitutes the "correct exposition of the holy teaching.

There is no subsequent section for a concluding explanation or for the dissemination of the text; this is likely because the author was different [from the standard format], and thus cannot be examined in detail.
There are three ways of explaining the reason for this: first, it is said that this treatise was composed entirely by Vasumitra from beginning to end;
although he praises his own virtues in the third verse, there is no fault of self-aggrandizement. Why is this so?
Because the Unsurpassed Dharma King has long since entered parinirvāṇa, and most other Arhats have likewise passed into nirvāṇa; as time progresses, human nature becomes increasingly degenerate.
All lack the eye of wisdom; if one does not personally declare one's own superior virtues, there may be doubt that the Dharma is not yet authentic.

Therefore, by citing one's own virtues, one manifests what has been taught so that it may be held in high esteem. Furthermore, since the Tathāgata accords with the holy and points toward the world as the Honored One, how much more so for a Bodhisattva who transcends the mundane?
Thus, one does not personally recount one's own lofty virtues; rather, virtue is manifested through the Way, serving as the standard for the person.
The supreme virtues are manifested because the person and the Dharma depend on one another; by extolling the Superior Person, the Dharma is made manifest.

Since he is called a Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa, his delusions and afflictions have long since vanished; thus, even though he speaks of himself, there is no fault of arrogance, as this is for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the Dharma.
The second [section] states: "The prose section extensively narrates the deeds performed by the Bodhisattva, followed by five verses."
The postscript was composed by a later scholar; for instance, he claims to be a bodhisattva endowed with great awakened wisdom.

How could one who internally harbors the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*) yet externally conforms to the nine realms of existence, who conceals his true state while flaunting his virtues in these degenerate times, be truly eminent?
Although he appears to propagate the Dharma, he suffers from the fault of self-aggrandizement. Thus, we know that the preceding verse was composed by a later scholar. The third [verse] begins:

According to such oral traditions, the final section—which concludes with the chronological listing of the chapters and the verses on the Bodhisattva’s deeds—along with the subsequent exposition of the fundamental principles and the core tenets, were all composed by later followers.

This is because the initial verses praise his own virtues, while the subsequent narrative fails to fully encompass the core tenets; thus, it is known that this treatise was not composed by the Bodhisattva from beginning to end.
The entire work consists of two main parts. The first five verses describe the decline of the various schools (*nikāya*) and set forth the true teaching so that one may rely upon it;
the subsequent prose sections explain the causes for the emergence of these schools and the tenets held by their different systems.
Regarding the initial five verses, they are further divided into three sections. The first two verses clarify the decline of the different schools and cause [the reader] to give rise to [faith].
Regarding the "Tiremy" (Aversion/Fear) section, there are two verses that reveal the excellence of the person who composed this treatise;
the subsequent verse encourages reflection on the Buddha’s teaching to distinguish the false from the true. Within these first two verses, there are again two sections:
the first verse clarifies the time of the schools' emergence and how it gave rise to decline and loss; the second verse clarifies how the schools arose according to their respective attachments.
To cause [beings] to give rise to revulsion and fear is the first [point]. Within this, there are two parts:

the first two lines clarify the time when the school arose, and the latter two lines clarify the decline of the school’s inception. "Buddha" is the Sanskrit *buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One.
Following ancient convention, the term is abbreviated and simply called "Buddha. He possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñā*), like a lotus flower.
To "open" [the mind] is like awakening from sleep; one is able to awaken oneself and also awaken sentient beings. When the practice of awakening is perfected, one is designated as a Buddha.
As for *parinirvāṇa*, this refers to "perfect stillness" (*yuanji*), which signifies the meaning of the perfect essence being quiescent and extinguished.

This demonstrates the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder). Following the period of the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), the Buddha remained for a long time, taking up these hundred years.

This would contradict correct reasoning; therefore, we now take only the entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. "Appropriate" (*śīghra*) signifies that not much time has passed, while "full" (*pūrṇa*) signifies the principle of non-deficiency.
If one did not say "appropriate" but spoke only of "full," then anyone who had not yet reached two hundred years would be considered "full" at one hundred.
Here, it is shown that even one hundred years is not long, hence the term "appropriate. This is what the old treatise refers to as "one."

One hundred years have already passed and sixteen more; if one does not say "full" but merely says "just," then "full" would not necessarily mean it is exactly full—it could also mean "just" [approaching] one hundred.
Now, because it is shown that one hundred years have been exceeded, the word "full" is used.

Furthermore, the word "exceeded" (or "remainder") is used to show that this is neither exactly one hundred years, nor is it a long-term completion, yet it is also not less than one hundred; such is the meaning.
This collectively reveals that the emergence of the various schools occurred just over one hundred years after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

"Ārya" (Noble) means "correct"; it is designated as "Noble" because it accords with correct principle (*nyāya*). Furthermore, it is called "Noble" because it accords with truth and penetrates the divine.
What is revealed by this term is that the teaching spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is capable of leading one toward the state of a Noble One (*ārya*).
The term "Holy Teaching" (*āgama*) means that which instructs, guides, and trains.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 126, states that the essence of the teaching is sound (*ghoṣa*), because it is sought throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and because it is of the nature of action (*karman*).

The expression "Holy Teaching" (*āgama*) indicates that it is not the teaching of non-Buddhist schools; it is so designated because the views and inclinations of the Tathāgata’s disciples differ [from others].

It is said: "Different classes of beings dwelling in separate places are further called 'sects' (*nikāya*); this refers specifically to differences among humans. "Arising" (*udbhava*) means "to originate.

This phrase generally indicates that within the Buddhist community, disciples have diverged and contended, resulting in the emergence of different sects; it does not refer to differences within non-Buddhist groups.
"Non-beneficial" (*anupakāra*) has the meaning of "decline and loss," referring to the impairment of the True Teaching and the loss of benefit for sentient beings.

The underlying meaning of this passage is as follows: When people are free from discord and the holy teachings are purely harmonious, the enlightened intent remains unerring and the Dharma suffers no decline.
Conversely, when people engage in conflict and competition, the holy teachings become diluted and estranged; as their emotional attachments and views differ, the Dharma falls into decay.

Since the distinction between what is correct and what is erroneous becomes difficult to discern, the holy teachings are allowed to languish, leaving sentient beings without a guiding authority upon which they can rely.
Delusion further prolongs the loss of the single flavor of the Golden Words, while the mixing of water and milk causes the human and Dharma to become diluted, thereby leading to decline and ruin.
Because heterodox schools arise within the Noble Teachings, they are able to bring about this lack of benefit.
These two lines generally clarify the decline caused by the emergence of schools; the intent of this verse reveals that [this occurred] during the time when the Buddha was present and...

Since one hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa, there have been no people who contend in discord and no teachings with divergent interpretations. This is because the Buddha and his noble disciples have sustained [the Dharma].
Thus, the Buddha possesses five qualities of sustenance: first, he is able to transform all those who are untransformable, such that there are no divergent sects among people;
second, he is able to sever the net of doubt, so that all doubts are resolved and there is no divergence in the Dharma.

1. Because he is revered by the three classes of beings—humans, asuras, and devas—and honored by those possessed of all virtues; 2. Because even if he were to give rise to a separate school, it would surely benefit the fourfold assembly;

3. Because the Dharma he teaches is certain to be beneficial; 4. Since the Dharma he has heard transcends worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), how could there be a separate adherence? 5. Because he can subdue heterodox arguments;

for he is able to subdue all Māras, external paths, and heretics, such that no person holds a different school and no Dharma possesses a separate adherence. Thus, the Buddha is endowed with these five [qualities].
Because the Dharma is upheld by virtue, there is no difference between the person and the Dharma.
One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, because it was upheld by the noble disciples such as Mahākāśyapa and others, there was no distinction between the person and the Dharma.

More than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, schismatic schools arose within the holy teaching, which gave rise to harmful matters; this serves to clarify that [the period of] one hundred years had already passed.
Although the Buddha has previously passed into extinction, no divergent schools have arisen within the holy teaching;
the sublime doctrine remains of a single flavor and in harmonious union, its integrity unimpaired, so that sentient beings of pure faith receive nothing but benefit.
Because they hold various differing views through successive transmission, as many schools as there are arise; based on their own Āgamas, they proclaim those attachments to cause revulsion.

This statement correctly clarifies that schools arise according to their respective attachments, causing [others] to feel weary of and terrified by them; the first half-verse demonstrates this "according to."
The "adherence to factions" (*pakṣagrāha*) refers to the subsequent explicit teachings that incite a succession of revulsion; it signifies the lack of certainty regarding [doctrinal] positions.

That which is accepted by one faction is rejected by another, and that which is rejected by one is accepted by another. Because these assertions and denials have no fixed master, they are said to be "mutually shifting.
The term "mutually shifting" indicates that their emotional views (*sattvadr̥ṣṭi*) differ. As for the word "because" (*hi*), it denotes causality. "Following" (*anu*) means to pursue or track.

As for their arising, it was due to the proliferation of various schools. Because the disciples mutually criticized one another and engaged in a cycle of acceptance and rejection, their emotional views became distinct.

Each followed his own intellectual understanding, causing the meaning of the teachings to become distorted. Lacking the mutual support of calyx and petals, they diverged into fragmented and discordant paths;
all followed their own emotional attachments to grasp principles and pursued their own intellectual interpretations. Since what each understood was inherently different, [the divisions arose].

The phrase "those who grasp" refers to those who subsequently differentiated into various schools; this demonstrates that these schools arose based on their respective attachments to personal opinions.
The preceding verse already mentioned that there are different schools within the Noble Teaching (*ārya-śāsana*); here, it clarifies how they originated.

*Āgama* is translated as "transmission," meaning that which has come down through successive succession; alternatively, it is translated as "teaching. *Vyāyāma* means "fear" or "detachment. This is the intended meaning of the Master [Vasubandhu].
This demonstrates that what is now being taught arises from our own internal convictions and is not a reckless or arbitrary fabrication;
rather, it is based on the fundamental teachings and the oral traditions of the Sarvāstivādins themselves. For what reason must this be taught? It is in order to engender world-weariness.
Thus, driven by the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, one has for three great eons, over a long period of time, firmly and fervently cultivated hundreds of thousands of practices as the cause.
Having fully realized the path of the perfect fruit to benefit sentient beings, he stirred the ocean of wisdom with his own ferry;

he expounded the True Doctrine to rescue all things, desiring that the mountains of delusion be naturally extinguished. With the sun of wisdom dwelling within his breast, he merged into the single source of principle, where the path to enlightenment is non-dual.

Thereafter, his disciples followed their own inclinations and gave rise to attachments, and as they pursued these attachments, various schools emerged, causing confusion and disorder throughout the eight directions.
Contending factions abound throughout the nine realms; the True Doctrine reaches the profound ultimate, yet it has been diminished by extraneous principles and frivolous doctrines.
The true essence lies in the primary meaning. Those who admire the Way hesitate between two extremes, and those who take refuge feel despondent at the crossroads.
Humans and devas have lost the way of reverent devotion, and the spirits and deities have ceased their virtue of solemn respect. This may truly be called a "tranquil ocean of wisdom."
That the wind blows against the bright sun of wisdom and mists shroud it is truly lamentable; it is truly a cause for grief!
That the masters of the treatises serve as the vessel for all beings and the beams and rafters of the Buddha-dharma, yet now find themselves so discordant, is deeply to be deplored.

Therefore, I rely on the transmitted teachings to provide a mirror and model for future worthies, so that they may know the Dharma is fundamentally without deviation, and that it is but human perception that sees differences—this is indeed to be rejoiced in.
One should not give rise to aversion toward the Dharma, nor harbor attachment to persons, nor produce fear; one should not be a leader in contention, nor be a pioneer in dispute.

Therefore, the second half of this verse is intended to engender aversion [to such disputes]. This single verse generally reveals that because the various disciples each cling to different views, various schools (*nikāya*) arose based on these distinct perspectives.
Now, in this world, Vasumitra, relying on the teachings of his own master, transmits their tenets.

You are able to seize the leaders of contention so that those in future generations may develop deep revulsion and fear; you shall always be the precursor to harmony and never the originator of the breaking of the Dharma.
The Great Bodhisattva Vasumitra, endowed with great wisdom, awakening, and insight, is a true Bhikṣu of the Śākya clan.

Regarding that time of contemplation and analysis, the commentary states: "The two verses below clarify the excellence of the person who composed this treatise. Regarding the contemplation and analysis of this [excellence], there are two parts:
first, one verse clarifies the excellence of the person who composed the treatise through contemplation and analysis; second, one verse clarifies the actual [composition].
Regarding the observation of those factors, it is appropriate to explain this; this is the first [section]. Within it, there are four parts:
(1) "Vasumitra" refers to the person who composed the treatise, by which the author reveals himself; (2) "the Great Bodhisattvas and others" indicates the superior virtues possessed [by the author];
(3) "of the Śākya lineage, truly... distinguishes his distinguished lineage; (4) "observing that time and so forth" refers to the correct contemplation and discernment, expressed as "Vasumitra."
The term "Vasu" is rendered in Sanskrit as *vaśumitra*. Here, *vasu* means "world" (*loka*) and *mitra* means "friend.

The god Viṣṇu, who is worshipped by the non-Buddhists, is also called *Vasu*, because he can save the world, because he is the father of the world, because he is the guide of the world, and because he dwells within the world.
Now, this author of the treatise obtained [this work] from him after having petitioned that deity.
Regarding the name "Vasumitra" (World-Friend): "Vasu" refers to a friend, such as when one speaks of Vasubandhu or Vasurāta.
Because he was the friend of Vasurāta, he was named Vasumitra. Furthermore, this deity was feared by violent and malevolent spirits and ghosts;

when the Bodhisattva was first born, his parents, out of tender affection, feared that he might be harassed by non-human beings, and thus gave him this name, saying: "This infant is [the friend] of the world..."
"O celestial friends, gods, and various spirits protected by the heavens, do not be afraid!
Just as this place is now designated as 'Protected by the Devas' (Shengu), where the deities guard and keep it in mind and non-humans do not approach;

so too, because this Bodhisattva’s great compassion rescues all beings and he is a friend to the world, he has thus designated his own name as 'World-Friend' (Lokamitra). It is not called 'Celestial Friend,' just as in the world [the former is used]."

Furthermore, because he dwells as a friend to the gods, he is called "Dwelling-Friend" (Mitāmitra). He is termed a "Great Bodhisattva" (*mahāsattva*) because his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) is already perfected;

thus, he is called "Great. "Bodhi" means awakening (*bodha*), and "sattva" refers to a sentient being (*sattva*). Because he is a sentient being endowed with the awakening of wisdom, he is called "Sattva.
He is able to seek *bodhi*, the awakening of omniscience, and takes all sentient beings as the object of his compassion.
Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva," it is explained as usual: this refers to a person who is conventionally designated (*prajñapti-pudgala*) as possessing [these] qualities.

As for the terms "great wisdom" and so forth, these reveal the three distinct qualities possessed: first, the quality of great wisdom; second, the quality of great awakening; and third, the quality of great insight.
By the word "great" applied to each—namely, great wisdom, great awakening, and great insight—"great wisdom" refers to the quality of benefiting others, while "great awakening" refers to...

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is twofold: the virtue of self-benefit consists in realizing the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is termed "Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*); realizing the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena is termed "Great Wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*).

Furthermore, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are assigned to these respectively. Alternatively, they may be explained as being sequentially assigned to the three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding specific characteristics, common characteristics, and so forth.
Moreover, "Great Knowledge" (*mahājñāna*) is the general awakening, while "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the particular; these two pertain to both oneself and others.
Regarding the specific application of the term "Śākyan" to the awakened wisdom: it designates the lineage of the Buddha; the Buddha belongs to the Kṣatriya caste, which is the Śākya clan.
This is translated as "Able. It is the clan of the ancient ṛṣis; because they are able to guide the world and possess the ability endowed with virtue, they are called "Able.
As for the term *bhikṣu*, it is sometimes named "Terrifier of Māra," sometimes "Destroyer," and sometimes "Beggar," and so forth, as described here.

The term "Śākya" (*śakya*) generally refers to the meaning of *bhikṣu* (monk), which applies broadly to outsiders as well; by now using the term "Śākya clan" (*śākyavaṃśa*), it is made clear that he is not an outsider.
Furthermore, while simply saying "Śākya clan" may include worldly laypeople, by now using the term "*bhikṣu*," it is made clear that he has left the household life.

Moreover, while the meaning of *bhikṣu* applies to both the noble (*ārya*) and the ordinary (*pṛthagjana*), by now making it clear that he is not ordinary, the word "true" (*bhūta*) is added. Finally, while the "noble" includes all three vehicles (*yāna*), [the text] here makes a distinction.
It is not dualistic; it is called "true" because this [path] leads exclusively to Buddhahood. "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to analytical observation.

"At that time" refers to a different period within the school (*nikāya*). Since the Master was born four hundred years after [the Buddha's passing], while the school dates from over one hundred years later, there is a considerable temporal distance between them.
Nevertheless, the term "that time" is used to indicate that he was reflecting upon the tenets of that specific school (*nikāyābhiniveśa*). "Discernment" (*vicaya*) refers to the act of deliberation.
This means that, having discerned and recounted the various competing tenets, the master Vasumitra—who possesses these virtues—contemplated the matter at the time those schools arose;
he analyzed the events and set forth the principles of the various doctrines. If one were not to manifest the virtues of the person, the Dharma would become subject to doubt;
therefore, by clarifying that the Dharma emerged from a superior person, its principles become reliable for faithful understanding, thus highlighting the person.

In order to encourage faith and practice, the Dharma is revealed; because it encourages one to follow the Dharma, it is necessary to cite the person [who realized it] to manifest the excellence of the Dharma.
Observing all the worlds, which are tossed about by various views, I shall explain the various doctrines according to the analytical teachings of the Muni.
The commentary states: What is clarified by this verse is that one should correctly contemplate those phenomena and acknowledge them as they truly are, which shall now be explained.

"Equality" (*samatā*) means either impartiality or pervasiveness. As for "the world" (*loka*), it refers to two types of explanations: first, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*); second, the container world (*bhājana-loka*).
Because these can be destroyed, they are called "worlds. To be submerged within them is what is meant by "the interval" (*loka*). Now, that which is here apprehended exists...

Regarding "sentient beings" (*sattva*), because they are not merely one, it further says "various" (*nānā*). "Views" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to perspectives; because these are not merely one, it says "of various kinds" (*vicitra*).
"Drifting" (*plava*) means floating, or it means surging; some say it means being swept away or drowning. "Wandering" (*saṃsāra*) means transmigrating, or it carries the sense of arising.
As for "view," it arises from persons, and persons follow after views; thus they are said to wander. "Muni" (the Sage) refers to this.

It is translated as "quiescent" because it pacifies afflictions, because it brings an end to birth and death, because one attains nirvāṇa through its quiescence, and because one realizes ultimate truth by quelling all conceptual proliferation.
Thus, the twelvefold teaching spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is called the "language of the Muni.
The phrase "this and that" does not refer to a single meaning; rather, it refers to the various views held by sentient beings.
Because they are adrift and wandering, [they] fragment the profound teachings on the fundamental meaning spoken by the Blessed One into various respective schools.

This intention is shown in summary: I have universally observed that among all classes of sentient beings, those who are leaders of contention are adrift due to their own views, while those at the tail-end of disputes are wandering due to the views of others—or [alternatively, the former are adrift due to their own views and the latter are wandering due to the views of others].

To reverse this, I shall now explain how these various heterodox schools—known as "those various [positions]"—arose from the power of causes and conditions that led to drifting and wandering at the beginning and end [of the teaching].
They divided the True Teaching spoken by the World-Honored One and established their respective sects. I shall now describe these twenty heterodox schools;

they are all called "those various [positions]" because they drifted and wandered according to their own individual views and understandings, thereby dividing the Buddha’s word. It is not [the case that]... [they are not the Buddha's word].
The Buddha’s words differ according to their origin and context;
one should carefully examine the Buddha’s teachings and rely upon the Noble Truths as they are proclaimed— just as one who gathers gold from sand selects only that which is real.

The commentary states: This verse clearly elucidates the exhortation to contemplate the Buddha’s teaching, rejecting the false and retaining the true. "Examination" refers to the thorough investigation of the Noble Truths;
"the teaching spoken by the Buddha" refers specifically to the instruction on the Four Noble Truths. It exhorts all sentient beings not to be swept away by their own biased views.
"True" means stainless and real, which signifies being firm and stable; one should carefully examine that which was spoken by the Buddha.

Within the teachings, only the instruction on the Four Noble Truths serves as the true locus of reliance: the two truths of suffering and its origin, which are the causes and effects of cyclic existence;
and the two truths of cessation and the path, which are the causes and effects of transcendence. These are real and not false;

there is no dispute among the various schools regarding this, and they are definitively such a truly reliable basis. Other peripheral doctrines and principles differ from school to school, their right and wrong being unsettled, like gathering flowers at random.
The "gold within the sand" is a metaphorical illustration. Just as one extracts gold from sand by taking the gold and discarding the stone, so too is it with the smelting of ore;
since the various scriptural teachings of the different schools are like gold ore, one should extract the gold and discard the ore.
The principle of the Four Noble Truths is like pure gold—true and not false—and thus should be relied upon, while all else should be discarded.

Whether a principle is correct or incorrect is ultimately difficult to determine; one should not follow one's own views and, due to mutual contradictions and disputes, slander other schools by claiming that none are entirely true.
Since there is no difference in the teaching of the Four Noble Truths among these various schools, one may rely upon and believe them.
This single verse generally clarifies this point; one should examine it with care, even though the interpretations of the various schools differ according to their respective tenets.
When views arise that should not be disparaged, these are simply the Blessed One’s teaching on the Four Noble Truths—true, real, and authentic.

Just as one who gathers gold and jewels from within sand relies deeply upon them and does not discard the gold because there is sand, do not discard the teaching of the Noble Truths because of the existence of disputes. These five verses collectively manifest the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa.
More than one hundred years later, heterodox schools arose within Buddhism, leading to its decline;
this was entirely due to their following their own personal views and fragmenting the Buddha’s teachings into various sects.

Now, as Vasumitra, I shall observe these matters and speak, exhorting all students to contemplate the Buddha’s teaching on the Four Noble Truths as being true and real, just as one would gather [precious gems].
Just as all the gold and jewels within the sand are neither discarded nor retained, so it is with the teachings of the various schools (*nikāya*).
One should take the teaching of the Noble Truths as the basis for study; as for other matters of dispute, one may accept or reject them at will.
One must not, following mere personal views, divide the schools and then universally repudiate them—this is the first account describing the decline resulting from sectarian differences.
This is the true teaching intended for one to rely upon when composing this treatise.
Such is the oral tradition.
The commentary states: From here on is the second section, which sets forth the reasons for the emergence of the various schools and describes the tenets held by different traditions.

The meaning of "intention" (*mata*) has five aspects: first, to manifest that it is based on oral tradition; second, to clarify the original teacher; third, to describe the era in which the school arose;
fourth, to relate how it split due to disputes; and fifth, to extensively present the tenets of the schools. This is the first [aspect].

Such a meaning unfolds according to four points, collectively indicating the meaning elucidated throughout the entire treatise. "Hearing" (*śruta*) refers to the arising of consciousness through the faculty of the ear.
"Listening and receiving" refers to what is heard by the ear; "hearing from tradition" (*paramparā-śruta*) indicates hearing through successive transmission rather than hearing directly.
What one hears and receives personally is called "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*); what is received from another is called "heard from tradition.

By first stating that [the teaching] is based on one's own *āgama*, it is shown that it is not a false statement; had this not been stated at the outset, it would imply that what was being taught was merely heard from one's own school (*sva-śāsana*).

Because there would otherwise be the delusion of presenting matters based on mere personal sentiment, it is called a "transmission" (*āgama*). To inspire faith in others, it is referred to as "heard by tradition.
[Thus speaks] the Buddha, the Bhagavat.

The commentary states: This is the second section, clarifying that the various disciples of the original Teacher after his passing debated the Buddha’s teaching, and not the teachings of non-Buddhists;
therefore, he is called the "Teacher. "Buddha" is explained as before. As for "Bhagavān," one who is able to destroy the four māras and possesses the six qualities is named Bhagavān.
More than one hundred years after the *parinirvāṇa*. [The commentary] states:
From here below is the third section, which narrates the dates of the emergence of the schools. Within this, there are five parts: first, a general narration of the year of the schism;
second, lamenting the corruption of the times through a metaphor; third, citing the locations where the schools emerged; fourth, identifying the lay protectors and kings; and fifth...
"Correctly setting forth the disputes of the time—this is the first [analogy], which can be understood according to the text.
'The time since the Sage departed has been long, like the sun having sunk for many days.
The commentary states: this is the second analogy, lamenting the corruption of the times; it refers to what was called 'the world' before the Tathāgata had yet appeared."
Since the Buddha-sun has already shone brightly for this Great Night, the world has finally been able to speak of light.

Had there not been guidance, how could those who are blind have conceived the hope of possessing the eye of wisdom? Since the transformation at the Crane Grove, the radiance of his awakening has receded into obscurity, and the world has likewise fallen into darkness.
As the years accumulate toward a full hundred, it is like the white sun setting in the west and the pale moon sinking in the east; as the night grows long, [the darkness deepens].
Because the world is profoundly dark and obscured, he raised a lament for the evils of the age as if the sun had long been submerged. In Sanskrit, this is called *asta*;
here it is translated as "submerged. *Udayana* simply means "rising"; it is not the name of a mountain where the sun rises or sets.
Thus, when people in the West today see the sun set in the west, they call it *asta*, and there is no separate mountain named *asta*.
The sun sets in the midst of the mountains; furthermore, the Sanskrit original merely states "more than a hundred years" and contains no mention of "sixteen years.
This tradition is an interpretation by later people and is not the actual text of the treatise.
In the kingdom of Magadha, at the city of Kusumapura. The commentary states:
this indicates the location where the school flourished. The name of the country in Central India is Magadha;
the name of the great capital city of the king is Kusumapura. "Kusuma" refers to the ancient capital city; there is a new capital city named Pāṭaliputra.
The son of Takṣaśilā, King Ajātaśatru, formerly resided in Rājagṛha; because his son and others had committed acts of rebellion and violence in the land of Rājagṛha, he moved the capital here.
Kusumapura was formerly called Aśoka; it was here that the capital was established.
Magadha—where the monks disputed—is here translated as "Free from Harm" (Aviṣama); it was formerly called "The Place Where Ambrosia is Attained" (Amṛtapada).

However, this meaning can also be understood as follows: In former times, the gods and the asuras were heavily afflicted by the poison of their own attachment, which caused their lifespans to be short.
Brahmā commanded them to use dragons as ropes and mountains as churning poles to churn the Ocean of Milk.
At that time, through the power of the merit of sentient beings, the ocean transformed into milk, and subsequently, it became sweet.
It is said that by wearing this garment placed therein, one attains longevity and is freed from all poisonous harms; thus it is called "The Harmless.

This is according to the interpretation found in the local customs of that region. Furthermore, as for Magadha, in the past during his causal stage, Śakra Devendra was known as "Nature-Loving-Soil-Treatment" (Kṣitigarbha-svabhāva);
together with thirty-two others, he made a vow and covenant at this very site to practice together.
Superior karma brings forth wealth and happiness in the present life, and subsequently leads to rebirth in the heavens;
it is named "Magadha" after its former state as the Śakra-devānām-indra. *Kusuma* translates here as "flower"; among the ten names for flowers, this is one such name.
If one speaks of the city of Kuśāgrapura, it means "City of the Tip of Grass," as auspicious grass grows abundantly in this place.
It is named "Auspicious Fragrance" (*Śāligandha*) for this reason; it is also said to be named "Flowers" (*Puspa*), as there are many exquisite fragrant flowers here, hence the name.
Furthermore, there is the city of Pāṭaliputra, which is connected to this place and situated slightly to its east.
Formerly, there was a Brahmin there who was highly capable and profoundly learned, with several thousand disciples. Occasionally, during his leisure time, he...
From the place where he was staying until he reached the Pāṭalī forest, there was a young scholar who wandered about in dejection.
His companions asked him, "Why do you have such a sorrowful countenance? He replied, "I have been traveling abroad for years and months, yet I have achieved nothing in my studies.

My appearance is still in its prime and vigor, yet I have no wife or concubine to cherish me. When I reflect on this, how could my grief not increase? The other students then stepped forward and teased him.
He said: "Now I shall arrange your marriage. We shall establish two persons as the father and mother for the groom, and likewise establish two persons as the father and mother for the bride.

We shall present a *māyūrapatrī* tree as the wife, pour water and offer flowers as the libation and food, express our sentiments to formalize the marriage rite, and determine the auspicious date for the union."
The scholar’s heart was filled with joy and contentment as he thought to himself that the day was drawing to a close and his fellow students were returning home.

Only this scholar remained, his feelings lingering and refusing to depart. While he stayed alone for the night and his friends had already left, the evening fell and the fires of the gods illuminated the wilds.
Amidst the songs and bells filling the banquet hall, suddenly an old man appeared, leaning on a staff, accompanied by a young maiden.
Wearing colorful robes, he stepped forward and the old man pointed to the young woman, saying, "This is your wife. They sang joyfully and played music for seven days.
His former disciples, all suspecting that a beast had harmed him, went to search for him;

they found him sitting beneath a tree as if conversing with a noble guest or meeting a distinguished visitor. When his companions requested that he return home, he declined their command. Afterwards, he himself...
He entered the city to pay his respects to his relatives and acquaintances, recounting the beginning and end of his story; everyone was filled with wonder and admiration.
After reaching old age, he fathered a son and said to his wife, "I now wish to return home, yet I cannot bear the thought of being separated from you.

I intend to stay here for a while, though my dwelling is but a temporary shelter in the open air. His wife spoke to her father, who replied, "In the pleasures desired by human life, why must one necessarily [seek them elsewhere]?"
"Since you are now building a residence in your native land, I hope you will have no other designs. Thereupon, he employed supernatural attendants, and the work was completed in a few days;
from that time on, the city took its name. *Pāṭalī* is the name of a tree, and *putra* means "son" or "offspring" of the tree;
because the city was established by means of the tree's offspring, it was named Pāṭaliputra. Thus, King Aśoka—

The son moved the capital to this location; the royal palace was situated to the west, for the most part in the former land of Kusumapura, while the populace was vast and entirely to the east, for the most part in the land of Pāṭaliputra, as its gates open toward the east.
Thus, the household follows the Master’s interpretation that Pāṭaliputra is mistaken for that [former] site. Furthermore, it is said there is a great kingdom named Pāṭaliputra.
This is also incorrect; this is the name of the capital city, so why call it a "country"?
Magadha is the name of the country. The ninety-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* also recounts this matter, saying:
"If Pāṭaliputra is taken as the country, then what is Magadha?"
The king, named Aśoka, ruled over Jambudvīpa; he was moved by a single white parasol to transform and govern both humans and deities.

The commentary states: this demonstrates the external protection provided by the human king. The first phrase lists the name of the king, while the subsequent three phrases manifest the king’s virtues.
Within the manifestation of these virtues, there are three parts: first, the breadth or narrowness of his domain; second, the auspicious omens that led to his becoming king; and third, his majesty.
Penetrating both the hidden and the manifest, this broad commentary explains the reasons why this king was so [as described] in the sutra.
This king was the grandson of King Bimbisāra. After Aśoka succeeded to the throne, his mind turned away from the Buddha-dharma;

his temperament became violent and impulsive, and he established hellish prisons to inflict harm upon living beings. It was only later, through an Arhat, that he first returned to faith—this being due to remote causes.
Regarding the offering of sand, it was recently through the conversion of the Noble One that his younger brother was delivered.
As described in the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), before the birth of Aśoka, this king’s father constantly feared that Candragupta would come to slay him;
however, on the day Aśoka was born, that enemy became his own enemy, and once the enmity was removed, the threat vanished.

He was named Aśoka, which means "Free from Sorrow. Furthermore, because this king’s countenance and deportment were beyond compare and his spiritual brilliance was peerless, he brought joy to his parents' hearts;
thus, he took "Aśoka" as his title. As for "ruling over Jambudvīpa," the extent of his domain—whether broad or narrow—is indicated by the name of the *jambu* tree.
This tree grows on the northern border of this continent near the water; the land is named "Jambudvīpa" after the tree.
The prince was large and handsome, and thus he was named accordingly. He was moved by a white parasol; this refers to King Śrīsaṃbhava.
When the king first ascended the throne, an iron wheel flew through the air—its hub red and its rim white, inlaid with various jewels—manifesting his power to subdue others.
A white cloud-like parasol covered Jambudvīpa; wherever it shone, that region was subdued, namely the entire world under one heaven.
That his transformation permeated both humans and spirits means that his majesty reached both the hidden and the manifest. "Permeation" (洽) carries the sense of moistening and soaking.
This refers to how the King thrice renounced Jambudvīpa to make offerings to the Triple Gem, causing all humans, ghosts, and powerful deities to construct eighty-four thousand exquisite stupas;
not only did his majesty subdue the common people, but his faith also transformed ghosts and spirits.
At this time, the Great Assembly of the Buddha’s Dharma was first divided.

The commentary states that when the formal dispute was being presented—specifically during the reign of King Aśoka in the city of Kusumapura in Magadha, more than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—the Dharma had not yet been divided. Prior to that [division], it remained as it was.
The harmony of the Buddha-dharma was disrupted;
that is to say, because the four assemblies deliberated together on the five points of Mahādeva, they disagreed and split into two schools.
The commentary states: from here below is the fourth section, describing the division caused by disputes, which contains two parts: first, clarifying the root cause.

Regarding the origin of the emergence of the sects based on this original dispute, there are two parts: first, the presentation of how various sects subsequently arose; second, the initial section, which has two sub-divisions.

The first sub-division is the general enumeration of the disputants and the disputed subject, divided into two groups. The second sub-division is the specific manifestation of the two groups divided into four assemblies and five matters.
This is the first [sub-division]: namely, "due to the four assemblies" refers to the disputants who collectively deliberated upon Mahādeva.
The "five matters that differ" refers to the points of contention. The "division into two schools" refers to the schism.
Below, the specific circumstances regarding the five matters of Mahādeva are set forth in detail.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Mathurā, there was a merchant leader who had married young and fathered a son of handsome appearance, named Mahādeva; not long after, [the following occurred].
In the meantime, the merchant master took his treasures and traveled far to another country, engaging in successive trade and failing to return for a long time.
His son grew up and became defiled by his mother; later, upon hearing that his father was returning, he became terrified in heart.

Together with his mother, he devised a scheme and subsequently killed his father. Having committed this one *ānantarya* (immediate) karma, the matter gradually became exposed, and he then spoke to her...
The mother fled in succession, hiding herself in the city of Pāṭaliputra. Later, she encountered a bhikṣu who was an arhat and received offerings from her own country;
fearing that her secret would be revealed, she devised a scheme to kill that arhat.

Having committed this second ānantarya crime, her mind became filled with grief and remorse. Subsequently, seeing her mother engaging in sexual intercourse with another man, she became filled with rage.
He said, "Because I served him, I have committed two grave offenses and been exiled to another country, wandering about in distress. Now he has abandoned me to seek someone even better than I.
Thus, with such foul and contentious speech, he was able to endure it; subsequently, through these means, he killed his mother.
Having thus committed the third *ānantarya* (immediate) karma, because of the power of his unsevered roots of goodness (*akuśalamūla*), [he did not fall into the Avīci hell immediately].
Deeply filled with remorse and unable to find peace in sleep or rest, he reflected upon his grave offense, wondering by what means it might be extinguished.
Having heard that the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, possess a dharma for extinguishing sins, he went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
Outside its gate, he saw a bhikṣu slowly coming out to perform walking meditation (caṅkrama), reciting a gāthā: "If a person commits a grave offense..."
Cultivating virtue to extinguish those [obstacles], he was like the moon emerging from the clouds that obscure it;
having heard this, he rejoiced and leaped for joy, knowing that by taking refuge in the Buddha’s teaching his sins would surely be extinguished.
Thereupon, he went to a bhikṣu and earnestly and persistently requested ordination. At that time, the bhikṣu, seeing his persistent request, did not examine him closely.

Upon interrogation, he was subsequently ordained as a monk; his name remained Mahādeva. Through instruction and admonition, Mahādeva—being of keen intelligence—was able, not long after his ordination, to recite and uphold the texts and meanings of the Tripiṭaka.
His speech was refined and elegant, and he was skilled at converting and guiding others.
There was no one in the city of Pāṭaliputra who did not look up to him with devotion. When King Aśoka heard of this, he summoned him and invited him to enter the palace on several occasions.

The King honored him with respect and made offerings, requesting him to preach the Dharma. Later, after he had left the monastery, due to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), he dreamed that he discharged impurity.
Since he had previously claimed to be an Arhat, he ordered his disciple to wash the soiled garment.
The disciple said to him: "For an Arhat, all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted; how can you, Master, now permit such a thing?"
While this matter still exists, Mahādeva declared: "You should not be surprised that you are being tormented by the celestial Māra.
There are briefly two kinds of outflows (*āsrava*): first, the afflictions (*kleśa*), and second, impurity (*aśuci*).
Arhats are free from the outflow of afflictions, yet they have not yet escaped the outflow of impurity. Why is this? Because all Arhats..."
Although afflictions have been exhausted, how could there not be such matters as the discharge of excrement, urine, tears, or saliva?
Yet, the various devas and māras constantly harbor hatred and jealousy toward the Buddha-dharma; whenever they see one practicing virtue, they go to destroy them. Even Arhats are disturbed by them;
therefore, these instances of my own physical emissions were caused by them. You should not harbor any doubt or suspicion regarding this matter. This is the discussion.

This is called the first [type of] wrong view arising from motivation. Furthermore, when that Mahādeva, desiring to cause his disciples to rejoice and remain devoted to him, deceitfully devised a stratagem and sequentially prophesied the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, his disciples prostrated themselves and said:
"The Arhats and others must possess realized knowledge; how is it that we ourselves have no such self-awareness at all? Thereupon, he...
He addressed them, saying: "O Arhats, there is indeed ignorance; you should not now lack faith in yourselves by claiming to be free from it.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of ignorance: first, that which is defiled, which Arhats no longer possess; second, that which is non-defiled, which Arhats still possess.
Because of this latter kind, you are unable to know for yourselves whether you have attained [Arhatship]. This is called the first [point of debate]."
When those two wrong views arose, the disciples spoke again to him, saying: "We have heard that the Noble One has already transcended doubt;
how is it that we still harbor doubts regarding the truth? He replied to them: "Even Arhats possess doubt, which is of two kinds:
first, doubt of the nature of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); [the Arhat] has [transcended this]."
The abandonment of the two [types of] doubt regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) has not yet been achieved by Arhats;
if even Pratyekabuddhas still possess them, how much more so for you Śrāvakas—how could you disparage yourselves when you are truly free from doubt regarding the Truths?
This is called the third evil view. Subsequently, his disciples read various sūtras stating that Arhats...
There is a noble eye of wisdom that can personally realize one's own liberation; for this reason, they said to their teacher:

"If we were Arhats, we should be able to realize it ourselves. Why is it that we must enter [the path] solely through the teacher’s command, while lacking any present wisdom capable of personal realization?
He replied to them: "There are indeed Arhats who enter [the path] solely through another."
Even Śāriputra, who knows for himself that he is foremost in wisdom and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers, would not know this unless the Buddha had predicted it;
how much less could one of dull faculties like you understand it by yourself without relying on another?
Therefore, you should not persist in interrogating him regarding this matter. This is called the fourth arising of a wrong view. Furthermore—

Although that Mahādeva had committed many evils, because he had not severed his roots of goodness, he later, during the middle watch of the night, reflected upon the gravity of his offenses and considered where he would have to undergo intense suffering.
Overwhelmed by anxiety and distress, he repeatedly cried out, "Alas, what misery!
When his resident disciples heard this, they were struck with wonder and alarm; in the morning, they went to inquire after his well-being, asking, "Mahādeva, are you not unwell?"
He replied, "I am very well and happy. His disciple immediately said, "If that is so, why do you cry out 'Alas, what suffering!
at night? He then told him, "I am calling upon the Noble Path; you should not find this strange.

Because the various Noble Paths will never manifest unless one calls upon them with utmost sincerity by crying 'Alas, what suffering!', I cry out 'Alas, what suffering! throughout the night. This is called the *kṛtsnāyatana* (the sphere of totality)."
Fifth, Mahādeva, motivated by these wrong views, later composed verses summarizing the five points of wrong view previously mentioned:
"One who is led by others, who is ignorant, who is hesitant, and who enters the path because of another’s voice—this is what is called the true teaching of the Buddha.
Subsequently, in the Kukkutārāma monastery, the majority of the *sthavira* bhikṣus gradually passed away.
Because he had passed away, on the fifteenth day at the time of the *poṣadha*, it was Mahādeva’s turn to ascend the seat and recite the precepts;

he then proceeded to recite a verse he himself had composed. At that time, among the assembly were those who were still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as those of great learning, those who upheld the precepts, and those who practiced meditative concentration.
Upon hearing what he said, there was no one who was not shocked and rebuked him, saying: "How clumsy! You foolish man, how could you even think to do such a thing?"

The commentary states: "The assembly of dragon-elephants" is a metaphor for those of the great devas' class. A "dragon" (nāga) is itself an "elephant" (hastin), and an "elephant" is also called a "dragon.

This has two meanings: first, their majestic power is irresistible; second, they are difficult to tame. Relying on the strength of kings and high ministers, they insult and treat with contempt the assembly of the Noble Ones.
Because of this, others fall into discord and strife; thus, their nature is such that their majestic power is irresistible.

Inheriting a nature that is cruel and obstinate, their practice of evil becomes increasingly severe; though the assembly of noble ones restrains them, they do not cease. Therefore, they are called "difficult to tame" (kūṭāvin).
They are of the same lineage as Mahādeva and are the leaders of strife and contention. As for the "border-dwellers" (pratyantaka), they are the disciples of Mahādeva and others;
because their mental conduct lies outside of principle, they are termed "border-dwellers," and because they possess no virtue worthy of mention, they are termed "vulgar" (pratyanta). This is so.

Since they are neither leaders of contention nor possess any formidable power, their names are listed merely as those from the borderlands who follow and support the faction of Mahādeva and his disciples.
As for the "assembly of the learned," these are ordinary practitioners and scholars who follow the sages,
who have profoundly mastered the subtle and profound, are extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka, and assist the virtuous faction.
To be called "one of great learning" (bahuśruta) means one who upholds the precepts, studies extensively, and serves as a support for the assembly of noble ones (*ārya-gaṇa*).

The "assembly of the virtuous" (*mahābhikṣu-saṃgha*) refers to the assembly of noble ones. Those who accord with principle, penetrate the divine, possess pure precepts and vast learning, and have attained unsurpassed loftiness of the Way—namely, the noble ones of the four fruits and so forth—are called "the virtuous. These four assemblies consist of two evil assemblies and two good assemblies.
Within these [groups], there are leaders and followers; Mahādeva and others are the leaders, while his disciples and so forth are the followers—these are the first two assemblies.

Within the assembly of the virtuous (*śubha-gaṇa*), there are likewise leaders and followers; the noble ones (*ārya*) are the leaders, while those who conform to the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are the followers—these are the latter two assemblies.
Furthermore, another explanation states that whether they be ordinary worldlings or noble ones, those who maintain the precepts with purity and loftiness are the virtuous.
Those who are skilled in the Vinaya-piṭaka are like fearless dragon-elephants; such holders of the Vinaya are called the "Dragon-Elephant Assembly," being the disciples of the Venerable Upāli.

Indeed, those who are not skilled in the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka are merely ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have broken [the discipline].

Whether ordinary or noble, those who wondrously understand the profound principles and deeply awaken to the subtle essence, possessing a Way worthy of praise, are called the Great [Sages].
The Virtuous Assembly consists of the disciples of the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, the great masters of the Abhidharma.

Furthermore, there is the Elephant-like Assembly: those within the monastic community who delight in initiating strife, who serve as a refuge for those who have broken the precepts, and who act as allies to the wicked;
