first, identifying the disputants and the schools from which they originated; second, identifying their place of residence; third, identifying the matters of discord and dispute;
and fourth, formally explaining the division of the schools. This is the first [section]. When two hundred years had passed, the previous schools were merely the second.
Within the hundred years, the period was not yet full; now, exactly two hundred years having passed, the school has been divided.

Thus it is said that at the time of completion, this was the final dispute within the Mahāsāṃghika. Among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), there are those whose appearance resembles that of laypeople and those whose appearance resembles that of renunciants;
since these are renunciants, they are called "renunciant non-Buddhists" (tīrthika-pravrajita) who have abandoned the ways of non-Buddhists.
The conversion of those following heterodox teachings to the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is also called "Mahādeva.

Regarding the statement that one hundred years prior there was a bhikṣu named Mahādeva who was the leader of a schism, the fact that he bears the same name as the present one is why he is referred to as "also" (api).
The explanation in the *Vibhāṣā* that this former Mahādeva went forth among the Mahāsāṃghika school serves to clarify [this point].

Regarding those who left the household life and received full ordination under a particular school, clarifying their status as members of the Saṃgha, upholding the complete precepts, studying extensively with superior reflection—this is what is meant by being "widely learned" (bahuśruta).
Their conduct was pure and lofty, and they were clearly designated as "diligent" (vīryavat). This discussion concerns their majestic virtue;
however, to clarify the school they followed, one must speak of the very head of the schism. Furthermore, there is an explanation stating that in the kingdom of Magadha...
King Haewon greatly propagated the Buddha-dharma; wherever he was, he made offerings to the great sages, who gathered in great numbers in his kingdom.

Both the nobility and the commoners of that land served only the śramaṇas and did not honor non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Consequently, the followers of non-Buddhist paths were destitute of the four requisites and were forced to secretly shave their heads to dwell as thieves within the monastic community.
Among them, there were some who were intelligent enough to receive and uphold the Tripiṭaka and were highly proficient [in its teachings].
The preaching of the Dharma had consequently caused ordinary people and sages to mingle, and the false and the true to be intermingled.
When the King learned of this matter, he purged those who were sages and ordinary people alike; many heretics and those dwelling as thieves returned to their own original sects.

Although there remained several hundred individuals who were sagely, enlightened, and broad-minded, capable of penetrating the profound mysteries of the Buddha-dharma together, the King asked the Sages: "As for these heretics dwelling as thieves..."
When the Holy One himself was present, he replied, "There are still several hundred;

those followers of the non-Buddhist path are extremely numerous, and if they were further eliminated, I fear they would destroy the Buddha-dharma. The King then had a separate monastery constructed to accommodate that group.
This Mahādeva was their leader, one who was widely learned and possessed great erudition.
He dwelt on Mount Caitya.
The commentary states: this clarifies that Mahādeva’s residence was named solely after its location. *Caitya* is what was previously called *zhiti*;
it is a corruption. This translates as "sacred shrine" (*lingmiao*), referring to a place where the holy spirit is enshrined.
Furthermore, because there were many caityas on this mountain, it was named accordingly.
When they deliberated again with the monks of that school on the five points, discord arose from this, and they split into three schools.

The commentary states: This clarifies the matter of discordant disputes. Mahādeva and the great assembly of the Saṃgha again deliberated upon the previous proposal regarding the five points of Mahādeva—whether they were acceptable or not—and because of this, the discordant dispute split into three factions. Below, the respective tenets are set forth;

from within [this section], it clarifies what was established. Although his reckoning of the five points was the same as that of the Great Assembly, he became distinct due to the discussion of these five points.

The division [of the schools] arose from disputes over other matters; the following enumeration of the five tenets established within this school shows they are identical to those of the Mahāsāṃghika.
First, the Caitīya school; second, the Aparasaila school; third, the Uttarasaila school.
The commentary states: Below this is the fourth section, which correctly clarifies the division of schools.
Mahādeva’s residence was named Mount Caitika (Caitraśaila), and its name is established according to the meaning explained previously. To the west of Mount Caitika is called the Western Mountain;
because he did not harmonize with Mahādeva, he resided separately on the Northern Mountain, which is likewise so named. This refers to a mountain located to the north of Mount Caitika.

All three derive their names from their respective locations; however, in the *Catuḥśāstrīya-vibhāṣā* translated by the former Master Paramārtha, only two divisions are mentioned—namely, the Bāhulika and the Uttaraśaila—and the same applies to the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā*.
Furthermore, that text adds the Pūrvaśaila while omitting the name of the Aparaśaila. These are all errors on the part of the translators, as will be understood below.
Thus, the four schisms or five schisms of the Mahāsāṃghika, when explained in detail according to their origins and developments, constitute nine schools.
The commentary states: what follows is the second section, which correctly lists the names of the schools divided; this section has two parts:
first, a summary of the four and five schisms, and second, the actual listing of the school names. This is the first part. Thus, as previously mentioned from the Mahā...
Among the various schools, there are four later schisms, namely those of the Ekavyāvahārika and the others; including the original [schism], there are five.

That is to say, from the time the Mahāsāṃghika first split from the Sthavira, whether considering the later or the original divisions, they are collectively said to be nine, though the later ones alone constitute eight.
According to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, if one includes the Mahāsāṃghika along with its root [division], [the count remains as stated].
To claim that there are only eight schools of the True Dharma (Satyasiddhi) masters, which together constitute seven schools, is entirely incorrect. [The eighteen schools are:
1. Mahāsāṃghika; 2. Ekavyāvahārika; 3. Lokottaravāda; 4. Gokulika; 5. Bahuśrutīya; 6. Prajñaptivāda; 7. Caitika; 8. Aparaśaila; 9. Uttaraśaila.

The commentary states: This is the formal enumeration of the names of the divisions as they were originally classified. According to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha taught that these combined divisions total twenty.
However, the translators of the *Mahāsāṃghika* school condensed them into eight, while those of the *Sthavira* school condensed them into twelve.
How do we know this is not the Sthavira tradition? Because apart from the Sthaviras themselves, the *Haimavata* school is mentioned separately.
Now, both the new and old schools maintain that the Sthaviras are also called the Himavat;
since there is no Sthavira school apart from the Himavata school, it is incorrect to say—as stated in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*—that the Sthaviras split into twelve.
This is because within the Sthavira school itself, they already speak of twelve branches, whereas the Mahāsāṃghika school speaks of eight in total. Among these...
Among the four divisions, one school—the *Anupaññatti-vāda* (or *Asaṃmatīya*)—is omitted;

furthermore, neither the old nor the new sectarian tenets mention the name "East Mountain" (*Pūrvaśaila*), which is merely an error by the translator. It should instead be called "West Mountain" (*Aparaśaila*).
This fails to realize that the *Sthavira* and the *Haimavata* split into two schools, while omitting one of the subdivisions within the *Mahāsāṃghika*. This is the teaching of Paramārtha.
The Master did not realize the number of schools and thus omitted two, speaking only of eighteen. Now, an objection is raised:

if you intend for there to be eighteen schools, why does the Sthavira school include both its root and branches when it is said to have eleven, whereas the Mahāsāṃghika school speaks only of its seven derivative divisions without mentioning its root?
If the Mahāsāṃghika were as they claim, how could it not be included among the eighteen schools?

If one says that the Sthavira school is also not included in this number, one might fear that there exists a separate Sthavira school apart from the Himavat school. Why, then, does the treatise you yourself translated state:
"The school residing in the Snowy Mountains is also called the Sthavira-śiṣya school"? Master Paramārtha heard such a tradition in his oral reports.
There are eighteen schools; if one were to say there are twenty, others might object, so [the author] omitted mention of the Mahāsāṃghika for fear of contradiction.
Furthermore, because he wished to establish his own count of eighteen schools, he reduced the number by merging the Aparaseliya school.

If the Mahāsāṃghika were included, there would then be nineteen. Consequently, the commentary states: "By combining the two divisions of the Tīrthikas into one, there are seven [schools]. This is the case.

This interpretation is incorrect. Why? Because according to both the *New Treatise* (*Xin lun*) and the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, when including the root schools, there are twenty divisions in total;
that is, even when including the root Mahāsāṃghika school, the count remains unchanged.
Thus, we know that the translation by Dharma Master Paramārtha is erroneous. It is simply because the root Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika schools are excluded that [the count] becomes ten.
Eighth, if the root schools are included, there are twenty; thus the Buddha’s prophetic declaration states: "The eighteen and the two roots constitute the twenty schools.
There is neither right nor wrong in this; I have said that they will arise in the future.

Regarding the translation [of these matters], one must be proficient in the languages of both oneself and others, understand the meanings of the various schools, and investigate their praises and criticisms; only then can they be known. Thus it is concluded.
Regarding the Sūtras of the Theravāda, for such a period they remained of one flavor and in harmony.
[The author] states: From here on, the second section clarifies the schools into which the Theravāda divided; therein are four parts:
first, showing that the Dharma was pure and correct and remained largely unified for a long time; second, showing how it split into schools due to disputes reaching the third century.
At that time, the Mahīśāsaka school arose; listing the names of the schools, this is the first.
The root of this school was maintained by Kāśyapa, and later it was assisted in its propagation by Upagupta, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Ānanda, and others.
Because holy ones succeeded one another, there were no disputes for two hundred years prior [to the schism]; therefore, it is said that for such a period of time, the Dharma was of a single flavor.
The phrase "revealing that the Dharma is without differentiation" clarifies that people do not engage in disputes.
At the beginning of the third century, there was a slight disagreement, resulting in the division into two schools.
The commentary states: "This refers to the second [period], from the second to the third century, when the schools were divided due to disputes; herein, some speak of two [schools]."
Since it was the beginning of the third century, more than a hundred years [after the Buddha’s passing], it is said to be the "start of the three hundred years.
The Sthavira school originally propagated the Sūtra-piṭaka as its primary focus, with the Vinaya and Abhidharma being propagated subsequently;
this does not mean they did not propagate the Vinaya and Abhidharma, but rather that they did not prioritize them. Then, at the beginning of the third century, Kātyāyanīputra...
When Loka appeared, he went forth in the Sthavira school; first he propagated the Abhidharma and later the Sūtras and Vinaya.

Since this deviated from the original intent of the Sthaviras, there arose disputes and turmoil known as "minor disagreements" (*alpavivāda*), which differ from the "great disagreements" (*mahāvivāda*) associated with Mahādeva.
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that Kātyāyanīputra was born at that time; rather, the distinction lies simply in their differing interpretations of the doctrine.

Consequently, they fell into discord and dispute; for instance, regarding the five propositions of Mahādeva, even though the Sthaviras still practiced them at that time, there were those who did not permit them.
Since this deviated from their original tenets, the school eventually split into two factions. What are these two factions?
First, the Sarvāstivāda, also known as the Hetuvāda; second, the Mūlasarvāstivāda, which was subsequently renamed the Haimavata.
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the third period, in which the sects arise; during this seventh period, the school is divided into seven sections.
"All that exists" (sarvāsti) means that all things are twofold: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The conditioned belong to the three periods of time, while the unconditioned transcends the periods of time; the essence of both is existent, and thus they are called "all that exists.
Because this school explains the meaning based on these reasons, it extensively analyzes them. It is named the Sarvāstivāda (School of All-Exists) according to its established tenet.
When they originally shared the lineage with the Mahāsāṃghika school, those of the Sthavira school who upheld the teachings of Kāśyapa changed their name to the Haimavata Sthaviras.
Their disciples primarily propagated the Sūtra-piṭaka, while the Hetuvādins emerged to extensively propagate the Abhidharma.
Once they became proficient in its principles and were able to subdue the monks of the Sthavira school, the Hetuvādins subsequently became very powerful.

Those who sit here [in the Snowy Mountains] are weak in their doctrinal exposition; based on their former residence, the Sthaviras moved into the Snowy Mountains, and thus they were named the *Haimavata* (Snow Mountain School) after their place of residence.
Alternatively, if the name is derived from the distant origin of the tradition, they are called the *Sthavira* (Elders).
Furthermore, in the terminology of the Western Regions, the winter season is called "snow-wind" (*hima-vāta*), as the wind of the snowy mountains prevails throughout the world.

Because it is designated as the "winter season," it is said that the snow-wind now blows. In this regard, the Sthaviras—the noble ones—are gradually diminishing and their tenets have become weak, such that people no longer propagate them;
whereas the Sarvāstivādins—the noble ones—are increasingly numerous, their principles are flourishing, and everyone studies them.
Thus, the Sthavira school has been abandoned and is no longer practiced; it is like the snow-wind, which signifies its weakness. Furthermore:
Since the Sthaviras are the root, they ought to have been placed before the explanation of the causes;
however, because their followers were few and their doctrine weak, they are listed later. Subsequently, during this third century, a school named [the Mahīśāsaka] emerged from the Sarvāstivāda.
The Vātsīputrīya school explains that "Vātsīputra" is the clan name of the Master of the Vinaya. In ancient times, there was a rishi who dwelt in a secluded mountain retreat;

The term "Vātsīputrīya" refers to a Brahmin clan. During the Buddha’s lifetime, there was a non-Buddhist follower of the Vātsīputra school who converted to Buddhism and left the household life, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Subsequently, his disciples transmitted this tradition without interruption;

It is said that the clan name of the Master of the Vinaya is indeed this. Master Paramārtha stated that the school of Kāśyapīya refers to the disciples of Rāhula;

They took the name of the school based on what Śāriputra had taught; thus it is called Kāśyapīya. Furthermore, it is said that in ancient times there was a seer (ṛṣi) named Kāśyapa.
