Because the people on earth were numerous, it is said that [the Buddha] transformed the earth; he abandoned his kingdom to leave the household life and extensively proclaimed the Buddha-dharma.

He was named after his original [role], hence the name Mahīśāsaka (Earth-Transforming School). Master Paramārtha stated that the Bhūmiya School (Correct-Earth School) was originally the royal preceptor who rectified the territory;
having abandoned that [position] to propagate the Dharma, they are called Bhūmiya. This is also somewhat similar [to the former explanation]. [This is recorded in] the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
To say that the Great [School] could not be abandoned is incorrect.
Subsequently, during this third century, a school named the Dharmaguptaka emerged from the Mahīśāsaka,
claiming that they inherited the lineage of the master Śiṣyaka.
The commentary states: "Dharmagupta" (法藏) is the name of the founder of this school; it is also called Dharmaguhya (法密). The meanings of "Gupta" (密) and "Gupti" (藏) are essentially the same.
Both the meanings of Dharmagupta and Dharmaguhya are applicable here, as this master contains and protects the True Dharma like a secret treasury;

thus he is called Dharmaguhya. The name of the founder of the school is established based on the person. According to the teachings of the masters of this school, there are five collections (piṭakas) in total.
1. Sūtra; 2. Vinaya; 3. Abhidharma; 4. Dhāraṇī—which clarifies various incantations and the like; 5. Bodhisattva—which clarifies the original deeds of the Bodhisattvas.
Since these deviated from the fundamental intent of the land of transformation, they subsequently divided the teachings.
Others, not believing this, cited Maudgalyāyana as proof. "Śu" refers to beans. In ancient times, there was a person who was fond of green [beans].
He gathered beans to serve as food and subsequently attained the state of an immortal; because Maudgalyāyana was born of that lineage of immortals, he is called "Bean-Gatherer" (*Mudgalāyana*).
Alternatively, it is said that the immortals eat beans, and this is their clan name—that is, their family lineage.
This section cites the words of Maudgalyāyana as proof that there are five internal organs (*pañca-kauṣṭhaya*).
At the end of the third century, a school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda named the Kāśyapīya, also known as the Bhadrayānīya.
The commentary states that "Kāśyapa" is a Brahmin clan name; it refers to the clan of Kāśyapa, which existed in ancient times.
The body of this immortal possesses golden light; when other lights come near it, they no longer appear because it swallows them up.
It is called "Light-Drinker" (Kāśyapa) because it eclipses all other light. Furthermore, as the founder of this school belongs to that clan, he is called Kāśyapa.

Moreover, the master of this school has a body of golden light capable of swallowing other lights, and thus he is called Light-Drinker. This teacher was virtuous and possessed of noble qualities from his youth.
He was given this name because he was born during a "good year" (*Suvarṣa*), as his parents praised his rare virtuous conduct;
thus he is called by his clan name, Kāśyapa, or by his personal name, Suvarṣa. Alternatively, it is said that during the Buddha’s lifetime, this was the son of Kālodāyin, whose clan name was Kāśyapa;
having joined the Buddha at a young age to renounce the world and receive the Way, he was named Suvarṣa.
For what reason do these people still exist at the end of the three hundred years?
At the beginning of the fourth century, another school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda, named the Sautrāntika, also called the Saṃkrāntika;
they claimed for themselves that they took Ānanda as their teacher.
The commentary states: This master relies solely upon the Sūtras as the authoritative standard (*pramāṇa*), not upon the Vinaya or the Abhidharma.

Whatever he cites as evidence is based on the Sūtras; thus, from the perspective of his established tenets, he is called the Sautrāntika (Sūtra-measure school), and is also known as the Saṃkrāntivāda (Proponents of Transmigration).
This master asserts that there exists a seed, and that this single seed alone continues to evolve in the present stream of consciousness.

Because it was transmitted to later generations, it is called the *Vyākhyā-prajñapti* (Explanatory Treatise); one should know that what was formerly called the *Śāstra-pāda* (Treatise Section) is this.
At the time of the First Council, the Venerable Ānanda specialized in propagating the Sūtra Piṭaka; since the Sūtras are now taken as the authoritative standard, Ānanda is regarded as the teacher.
The name of the school is derived from the person who established it: Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra propagated the Abhidharma, while Upāli closely adhered to and propagated the Vinaya.
Since they no longer rely upon the Abhidharma and the Vinaya, they now take Ānanda alone as their teacher.
Thus, the seven or eight schisms of the Sthavira school, when distinguished by their primary and secondary branches, constitute eleven sects.
The commentary states: From here below is the fourth section, which summarizes and lists the names of the schools. This section has two parts: first, clarifying the number of schisms;
second, the actual listing of the names. This is the first part. If one includes the schism from the Sthavira and the Mahāsāṃghika, there are eight schisms in total.
If one excludes the fundamental [schisms] and speaks only of the derivative ones, starting from the Sarvāstivāda, it is as follows:
Because there are seven schisms, when combined with the fundamental [schism], they constitute eleven schools;
including the separate schism mentioned in the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* along with the fundamental one, there are twelve schools, as already reconciled previously.
1. Sarvāstivāda; 2. Haimavata; 3. Vātsīputrīya; 4. Dharmottarīya; 5. Bhadrayānīya;
6. Saṃmitīya; 7. Caitīya; 8. Mahīśāsaka; 9. Dharmaguptaka; 10. Kāśyapīya; 11. Sautrāntika.
The commentary states: This section, which correctly lists the names, is clear from the text.
I shall now explain the fundamental tenets (*mūla-siddhānta*) and derivative tenets (*uttara-siddhānta*), as well as the common and divergent doctrines of these various schools.
The commentary states: From this point downward is the fifth major section, which extensively presents the sectarian tenets; it contains two parts, the first of which is the general introduction.
It is permitted to explain the subsequent sequence by presenting them individually; this is the first [point]. In this manner, these various schools cite the preceding schools.
Among these, the "common tenets" (*sādharmya*) of the fundamental school and the "distinct tenets" (*vaidharmya*) of the derivative school are as follows:

for instance, at the time when the four root schools—the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Gokulika—first established their positions during their initial dispute, the name of the tenets they shared in common is...

Regarding the "Sectarian Schools with Identical Tenets" (Samāna-dharma-vibhāga) within our own school: after the initial establishment of tenets, those subsequently established separately within the same school that diverge from what was initially established are called "Sectarian Schools with Identical Tenets" (Samāna-dharma-vibhāga).

This is like the Mahīśāsaka school, which emerged from the Mahāsāṃghika; at the time of its initial emergence, the tenets it established were named "Sectarian Schools with Identical Tenets," and thereafter [those that diverged] were distinguished as "Different Tenets" (Vilakṣaṇārtha). Furthermore, it is like the Saṃmitīya school, which arose from the Mahāsāṃghika; at the time of its initial emergence, the tenets it established were named "Sectarian Schools with Identical Tenets," and thereafter...

Furthermore, there are other distinct establishments that deviate from their original intent; these are termed "Divergent Doctrines" (*mūla-siddhānta-vipratipatti*) and should be understood accordingly in each and every section.

However, within this present work, I shall generally introduce them at the conclusion [of each section]. In those concluding sections, some will recount both the original and divergent doctrines, while others will recount only the original or only the divergent;
as for those whose meaning is identical to others, I shall not describe them further to avoid prolixity. This is the case here.

I shall now explain the points of agreement among the various schools' fundamental tenets and the points of divergence among their derivative tenets; I shall first state what is accepted and subsequently state what is to be explained.

"Now" refers to the present time; "in this treatise" means within this work; "shall explain" (*bhaviṣyati*) is used because it follows the word "subsequently" (*anantaram*), hence it is called "shall.
This constitutes the first general heading stating what is accepted and what is to be explained.
Regarding this, the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Gokulika schools—those who share the same fundamental tenets—state as follows:
[The commentary] says: From here below, the second section presents the individual enumerations in sequence. Although there are twenty different schools, they are combined into eleven sections;
for the three schools—the Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Gokulika—are collectively grouped with the Mahāsāṃghika.
The various schools are grouped together for narration: the two schools of the Western Mountains (Aparaśaila) and Northern Mountains (Uttaraśaila) are combined with the Caityaśaila school;
the Dharmottarīya, Bhadrayānīya, Saṃmitīya, and Kṣadraka schools are combined with the Vātsīputrīya school. Thus, there are eleven sections in total.
Within each section’s exposition of the doctrine, there are two parts; here, in the first instance, the schools are identified and their fundamental tenets are introduced.

Section Two: A Separate Presentation of the Tenets Held by Each School. This section first indicates the schools and then sets forth their fundamental tenets. Having completed the general overview, the following is the specific presentation.
That is to say, the four schools all maintain that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are all supramundane beings.
The commentary states: From this point downward, the specific exposition is given; however, where it differs from other schools, these points will be addressed one by one as the text is explained.
According to the intended meaning of this school, the body of the World-Honored One is entirely supramundane and cannot be surpassed, for it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are termed "mundane" (*loka*) due to being subject to destruction and inferior to the noble ones (*ārya*).
The learners (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles surpass the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), yet they are inferior to those who have attained non-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The non-learners of the two vehicles surpass the learners, yet they are inferior to the Buddha. Their bodies are not "transcendent" because they are exclusively outflow-free (*anāsrava*);

they are not "indestructible" because they still bear the name of "worldly existence" (*loka*). Only the World-Honored Buddha surpasses all others and possesses nothing inferior; therefore, he is truly indestructible.
That all things exceeding destruction are supramundane is a discourse concerning persons based on the untainted body;
therefore, the interpretation of the Sarvāstivādins and others is incorrect. All Tathāgatas possess no tainted dharmas.
The commentary states: Regarding the treatise on the dharmas, when the eighteen *dhātus* and so forth exist within the body of a Buddha, they are all termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
Because they are neither associated with outflows nor bound by outflows, they are called outflow-free. All three types of action (*karman*) belonging to a Buddha are likewise outflow-free;
therefore, the Tathāgatas possess no outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Apart from these four categories, the remaining categories [of the Buddha's qualities] are... [the Buddha].
None of these [limitations] apply.
The speech of all Tathāgatas turns the Wheel of Dharma.
The commentary states that because all speech spoken by the Buddha constitutes the Wheel of Dharma, the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma is not limited solely to the Eightfold Path.

The Bhadrayānīyas claim that the eight branches of the noble path constitute the true Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), and that it is not the word of the Buddha to say that the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) alone is called the "wheel" in the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. This school asserts that it is not only the Path of Seeing that is designated as the wheel;
for there is no word spoken by the Buddha that is not beneficial, and thus everything spoken by the Buddha is the Wheel of Dharma, characterized by its power to crush, subdue, and turn.
It is called a "wheel" because the Buddha’s speech revolves within the bodies of others, having already subdued the ignorance and delusions within those bodies;
therefore, it is termed a "wheel. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Did it rain? and asked the bhikṣus, "Are you at ease? What benefit is there in this?
It is called the Dharma-wheel. [The Buddha] replied: "All of these are for the sake of benefit, so as to cause Ānanda to attain clear discernment."

Since there is nothing the Buddha does not know, why would he still ask about the rain from the heavens? How much more so for one whose wisdom is not yet perfected—would he not examine things with careful scrutiny?
It is because the Buddha wishes to eliminate the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) of others that, though he knows, he asks; how much more so for those who do not know?

Regarding other dharmas whose nature and characteristics are not yet understood, would they not fail to examine them with careful scrutiny? For many such reasons, he questioned the bhikṣus: "Are you well-adjusted?"

It is not that [the Buddha] lacks compassion; rather, had he not asked, it would have been thought that the Buddha lacked compassion because he did not know whether his disciples were safe or in peril.

He therefore asked questions in order to cause the bhikṣus to joyfully cultivate the Path, so that they might train with great joy, and also so that those in the future might practice this same thing, just as [in the present].
For these various reasons, all that the Buddha speaks constitutes the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
the essence of this wheel of Dharma consists precisely of the Buddha’s teachings in the form of names, phrases, and sounds.
The Buddha expounds all dharmas with a single voice.

The commentary states: Through the spiritual power of the perfected merit cultivated over a long period of time, as recorded in the Buddhist sūtras, which transcends all conceptual thought, he utters a single name with a single sound, causing all sentient beings to hear the Dharma and each individually eliminate their own defilements.

As for the objection that [a single sound] can express all dharmas and cause all hearers to individually comprehend both coarse and subtle meanings, the Sarvāstivādins and others do not accept this; however, this shall be understood in detail below.
"Nothing spoken by the World-Honored One is not in accordance with the truth.
The commentary states: "The words spoken by the Buddha bring benefit to others; there are no empty words or those that do not bring benefit.

"Truth" (yi) refers to purposeful benefit (*artha*), because all such things are thoroughly beneficial. The Sarvāstivādins and others claim that even the Buddha, the World-Honored One, sometimes speaks what is not in accordance with the truth.
This is because it accords with the meaning. Furthermore, all that the Buddha has spoken is free from error and conforms to reason;
it cannot be subject to refutation and is thus called "in accordance with the meaning" (*yathārtha*). Moreover, there are four kinds of faults absent in the Buddha’s speech:

first, no inappropriate place; second, no inappropriate time; third, no inappropriate recipient; and fourth, no teaching that is not the Dharma. "Place" refers to a location where benefit should be conferred.

"Place and time" refers to the specific occasion when there is benefit; "vessel" refers to the appropriate capacity; and "Dharma" refers to the teaching—such as morality, concentration, and wisdom—which are the dharmas that should bring benefit.
One must certainly not speak erroneously regarding these.
"The form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata is truly without limit.
Commentary: The intention of this school is that the *sambhogakāya* attained by the Buddha through cultivation over many kalpas is perfectly consummate within the *dharmadhātu* and has no limits;
as for the [image of] sixteen feet seen, it is not the true Buddha-body, but a transformation manifested according to the capacities of sentient beings. — Master Paramārtha.
It is said that the Buddha’s body has three kinds of boundlessness. First, boundlessness of measure:

because he manifests bodies of large or small size according to what is appropriate for beings, there are cases where he is small and no longer large, or large and no longer small; thus it can be said that his body has limits.

However, since one cannot definitively state that the measure of his body is only large, it is called "boundless. Second, boundlessness of number: if there are many sentient beings who, at one and the same time...
Each should see the Buddha; for the Buddha is able to manifest many bodies, and since the number of these bodies is not fixed, they are said to be "boundless.
[The claim that] the Buddha-bodies have "boundless causes" because each and every phenomenon arises with immeasurable roots of goodness as its cause is incorrect.
This principle is not so, for schools such as the Sarvāstivāda also maintain that these three [qualities] are boundless.

What is the distinction regarding these limits that is now being described? The intended meaning here is that the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is without limit and differs from those of other schools;
therefore, it is described separately. To verify this single principle, although various principles may differ, they shall not be described extensively one by one in their particular distinctions.
The majestic power (*anubhāva*) of the Tathāgata is likewise boundless.

The commentary states: This school explains that all the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) possessed by the Buddha are termed "majestic power" (*anubhāva*), because they consist of majesty, virtue, and spiritual power;
thus they are called "majestic power. It is said that without deliberate effort (*amanasikāra*), in a single moment, he can pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Various schools maintain that when the Buddha does not direct his attention, he reaches only the trichiliocosm, whereas when he does direct his attention, he can pervade the ten directions.
Now it is said that even without directing his attention, the Buddha can pervade the ten directions; thus, Master Paramārtha has already provided an extensive citation [of this point].
The lifespan of all Buddhas is likewise boundless.
The commentary states: Because the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) is attained through cultivation over infinite eons, its actual life span is also inexhaustible.

For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they cultivate the path for many eons; as long as the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, their life span remains infinite for the purpose of providing benefit.
Since sentient beings have no day of rest, if he were to transform them according to their needs, he would likewise remain hidden in the twin śāla trees;

if he were to extend his lifespan by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), how would this differ from other schools? Now, because it is taught that his life is real, it is distinct from other schools in being without limit.
The Buddha transforms sentient beings, causing them to give rise to pure faith, yet he possesses no mind of weariness.
The commentary states: "The Buddha transforms sentient beings, causing those beings to develop deep faith and joy; the Buddha has no mind of weariness.
The intended meaning of this school is that because the Buddha’s mind of benefiting others is never satiated, he does not enter nirvana out of his compassion.

With infinite life and no limit, if there are sentient beings for whom the Buddha’s manifestation would bring benefit and peace—such as those born into royal palaces and the like—and who require guidance through the process of attaining Buddhahood, he manifests accordingly. When the conditions for such manifestation cease, he enters parinirvāṇa.

Because his mind never knows satiety, he retains his *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) until the end of the future, manifesting forms according to the various classes of beings to teach them through skillful means.
The transformation speech is never satiated, unlike other schools which manifest it only until the conditions for transformation are exhausted;
[in those views] the true reward body enters eternal quiescence, implying the mind has become weary.
The Buddha, however, has neither sleep nor dreams.
The commentary states: Sleep is a state of mental dullness and contraction that occurs only in the distracted state; since the Buddha has no unconcentrated mind, he has neither sleep nor dreams.
Because dreams are produced by conceptual thought, desire, and so forth, and the Buddha lacks such conditions, he likewise has no dreams.
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that while the Buddha experiences drowsiness (*middha*), he has no dreams, because he lacks the arising of false thoughts or desires.
Because the Buddha is free from the obscuration of undefiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) which can induce dreams, his dreams do not occur;
furthermore, since certain schools admit that the Buddha has dreams, it is said in combination that the Buddha is without sleep or dreaming.
The Tathāgata answers questions without depending on deliberation.

The commentary states: The intention of this school is that the Buddha has no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and does not deliberate upon the names, phrases, and syllables to be spoken before speaking to others;
rather, he is able to answer spontaneously. Other schools maintain that although the Buddha lacks intentional effort and preparatory application, [he still speaks].

[The Buddha] answers others' challenges by means of names, phrases, and syllables as they arise from conditions; however, in this case [of the Buddha's spontaneous speech], it does not depend on deliberation.
Because the Buddha never speaks names and so forth at any time, remaining constantly in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), sentient beings nevertheless perceive him as speaking names and so forth.
With great joy and exultation, he remarked:
"The intention of this school is to say that when the Buddhas teach the Dharma, they do so spontaneously;

there is no need for deliberation regarding names, phrases, or syllables. Their spontaneous and self-arisen, rational teachings consist of excellent names and phrases, which are always present within meditative concentration."
The Buddha does not intentionally contemplate names and so forth; however, for those who listen to the Dharma, the Buddha appears to contemplate names and so forth as he proclaims the teaching.
When such reasonable words and instructions manifest before them, they give rise to immeasurable joy and exultation, and by relying on these teachings, they practice accordingly.
This is the meaning of accomplishing the task spontaneously without intentional thought—that is, the Buddha does not intentionally contemplate names, phrases, or syllables.
Spontaneously and naturally accomplished, the supreme names, phrases, and syllables are what sentient beings call "the Buddha";

it is only because he first contemplates these names and so forth that he subsequently teaches them, and they rejoice and celebrate, practicing with leaping vigor. This is not the case for other schools;

for even though the Buddha lacks applied effort or deliberation, he nonetheless contemplates the names and so forth to be spoken, arranging them according to the Dharma before teaching them to others.
This statement differs from that of other schools.
[It asserts that] "a single momentary mind comprehends all phenomena.

The commentary states: "With the exception of the Buddha, although the minds of others take common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) as their objects, even a single momentary mind can also take intrinsic nature (svabhāva) as its object."

Although [the Buddha] understands all phenomena, he cannot realize their specific distinctions; therefore, throughout many kalpas, the Buddha refines his mind through the training of the Buddhas' scriptures.

Because there is no one who surpasses the Buddha in understanding all minds, the Buddha’s single momentary thought can understand the specific natures of all phenomena and realize them, whereas the minds of other classes of beings cannot understand even one in a single thought-moment.

While all phenomena exclude their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as well as associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) factors, this single momentary thought also discerns the distinctions among the intrinsic natures of its own nature, associated factors, co-existent factors, and so forth; thus, it differs from other schools.
The Prajñā associated with a single momentary mind knows all dharmas.
[Commentary: This clarifies that at the time of a single momentary mind, the Buddha’s wisdom is also able to understand and know all dharmas completely and perfectly;
thus, it extends through the final single thought-moment following the Path of Liberation and the Vajra Path.
One is immediately able to understand that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena does not depend on a continuous succession in order to be known as exhausted;

one also understands the intrinsic nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, while it was previously explained that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) cognizes the exhaustion of phenomena, it is now explained that the function of wisdom in understanding the exhaustion of phenomena is no different.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly follow [the Buddha] until his parinirvāṇa.
[Commentary: According to these schools, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of the Buddha are all untainted (*anāsrava*).
The Buddha’s untainted wisdom is constantly manifest at every single moment until his parinirvāṇa. In this school, there are two types of knowledge, namely, the knowledge of exhaustion...
The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is precisely the contemplation that present suffering is extinguished, which is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*);
it is the contemplation that future suffering will not arise, which is called the knowledge of non-arising. At all times, these two functions of a single essence revolve in constant conjunction;

thus, these two functions are explained as the two knowledges manifesting before one. If even a Buddha, according to the Sarvāstivādins and others, still possesses indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states of mind, how much more so these two?

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that these two knowledges arise constantly; because they are ever-present within the body of one whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*), they are called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*);
and because they are ever-present within the body of one who has attained non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they are called the "knowledge of non-arising.

While this may be the case for the Sarvāstivādins and others regarding the bodies, it is not so for the knowledges themselves; therefore, this constitutes a point of difference. [Question: What was previously clarified regarding the absence...?

Question: It is said that the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is inexhaustible; for what reason is it said that the two types of wisdom manifest until *parinirvāṇa*, while the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) undergoes *parinirvāṇa*, but the *saṃbhogakāya* does not? Answer:

Although it is true that the *saṃbhogakāya* has no day of entering *parinirvāṇa*, even if the realm of sentient beings were to be exhausted at the end of the future limit, there would still be a time of *parinirvāṇa*. However, [the *saṃbhogakāya*] never ceases.
The fact that the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) constantly functions alongside [the other two knowledges] indicates that these two knowledges are uninterrupted;
it does not indicate that the *saṃbhogakāya* has a day of entering *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, when all Bodhisattvas enter the mother’s womb, they do not take up the *kalala*, *arbuda*, or *peśī* stages.
*Kalala* constitutes the self-substance.
The commentary states: *Kalala* means "impurity"; it refers to the impurities of the father and mother. Because it is a mixture of defilements and is loathsome, it is called "impure.
*Arbuda* means "bubble"; as it gradually thickens and coagulates, it resembles a blister or scab. *Pesi*.
*Śi* (尸) here means "coagulated" (*nigata*), while there it is called "cooked blood" (*pakvarudhira*). It is also said that after being enclosed for days, it gradually grows and becomes coagulated.
*Kian-nan* (鍵南) here means "thickening"; it refers to the gradual thickening of the coagulation. The *Pañcarājāsūtra* states: on the first seven days it becomes impure matter;
on the second seven days it is like a blister; on the third seven days it has become coagulated; and on the fourth seven days it gradually thickens.
When a Bodhisattva enters the womb, he does not rely on impurity, nor does he undergo this gradual growth;
rather, upon entering the womb, his sense faculties (*indriya*) and great elements (*mahābhūta*) are already fully present.

Since all are instantaneously perfected, from the stage of *kalala*—which is called "possessing the faculties"—up to the fifth week, this period is designated as such, thereby revealing that the Bodhisattva possesses a distinct purity.
The pure derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and primary elements (*mahābhūta*), together with the sense faculties (*indriya*), are suddenly complete as its own substance;

it does not employ the impure, and therefore it does not grow gradually by being nourished by the impure. This gradual growth occurs during the preceding four stages, at which time it undergoes oppression.
Question: Is this Bodhisattva in his final body, or is he [in an earlier stage]? Answer: Here, one [type] is being described.
For all Bodhisattvas in their final existence, regardless of their previous stages, it is not necessarily the case that they always take this form;
however, when all Bodhisattvas enter the mother's womb, they manifest in the form of a white elephant.
The commentary states: This section explains that there is absolutely no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). As for this form of a white elephant, what kind of entity is it?
The intention here is to clarify that the form of the white elephant is the sign of entering the womb; it is not the body of an intermediate state being.

It is not meant to say that the intermediate state of a Bodhisattva or a noble one transforms into that of an animal; rather, it is because the elephant is by nature docile, lacks violence or ferocity, and possesses great majesty.

Because his power is like that of the well-established dragon, he manifests this appearance; the intention is to signify that the Bodhisattva’s nature is inherently gentle and harmonious yet possesses great power.
Although the lion king and others possess majestic might, they frequently inflict injury and slaughter; therefore, the Noble One does not manifest the form of a lion.
According to the Master of Dharma, although there is a broad interpretation regarding the white elephant form, it is stated here that—

Among the Bodhisattvas, there may be those who fear a deviation from the fundamental tenets, for this school’s own primary doctrine holds that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*); those who investigate will know this for themselves.
Furthermore, when all Bodhisattvas emerge from their mother’s womb, they are born from the right side.

The commentary states: Māndhātṛ was born from the crown of the head, for he possessed the most excellent merit among men; others were born from the head, neck, or other parts, being summoned by inferior karma.
He emerged through the lower gate. Having transcended worldly things in his bodhisattva stage, his path lies beyond the mundane;
free from biased attachments, he constantly treads the Middle Way. To manifest this, he was born from the side; thus the mother carrying him in her womb was free from the distress of pregnancy.
Furthermore, when emerging from the armpit, there was no pain in the abdomen; he emerged from the side in accordance with the *Līlāvatāra-parivarta*. Question:
Since the sides are both left and right, why did he not emerge from the left? Answer: The relative importance of the left and right is not fixed across all regions. In this land, the left is honored;
in the Western lands, the right is honored because it is considered auspicious. Therefore, he emerged from the right. Question: Was there also pressure within the Bodhisattva’s womb?
"Constricted" refers to the various evil conditions of darkness, ignorance, and foul impurity. The answer is that there is not a single place [there] that is constricted:

first, it is vast and great; second, it is eternally luminous; and third, it is utterly pure. This represents that after birth, one is likewise free from three conditions: (1) the analogy of the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) represents the state of being constricted;
(2) the analogy of birth and death is like the darkness of night; and (3) once Bodhi has been realized, the disturbances of Māra and his hosts are like the foul stench.
Because they are free from defilement, Bodhisattvas are entirely devoid of such things as oppression and the darkness of ignorance.
No Bodhisattva gives rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of malice, or thoughts of harm.
[The commentary] states: This section explains that upon entering the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one is immediately named an Ārya; from this point onward...
Afterwards, even throughout a hundred kalpas, he would not again give rise to these three kinds of perceptions; how much less would he give rise to the three perceptions in his final body?
Even though other schools permit that a Buddha might give rise to them, [this is not the case here].
Bodhisattvas, desiring to benefit sentient beings, can go to the evil realms at will, even if they have made vows to be born there.

The commentary states: While other schools maintain that those who have attained *kṣānti* (receptivity) and beyond are no longer reborn in the evil paths, this school asserts that even those who have attained the state of an *ārya* (noble one) can still be born in those realms by their own vow. This is just as the *Śālistamba Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings are born [according to their karma]."
1. Delighting in the Bodhisattva’s birth in the miserable realms (*durgati*): since all births therein are suffering, even if it be little, the mind feels increased revulsion and fear;
if one repeatedly experiences such suffering, the mind of revulsion increases. 2. For the sake of impartial rescue:

if one were to rescue only those in the happy realms (*sugati*) and not those in the miserable realms, the mind of liberation would be partial and thus unequal. 3. Firm endurance: if there were no time of suffering, [the practice] would be like...
How so? Because the Bodhisattva of Endurance possesses great compassion and sovereign supernormal powers, he goes wherever he wishes as soon as his vow is made;

thus, "going here" is named after "going there," and the same applies to the stages of birth, abiding, and death, for all are characterized by sovereignty. Furthermore, there are three stages for a Bodhisattva: first, the stage of non-fixation, which is the first eon;
second, the stage of fixation, which is the second eon; and third, the stage of receiving the prediction [of enlightenment], which is the third eon.
Although they had made the vow at the beginning of the eon, they were not yet born in those two subsequent states; however, once born there, they could go at will.
In a single kṣaṇa, through the knowledge at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya-antika-jñāna*), they thoroughly understood the specific characteristics of the Four Truths.

The commentary states: This refers to the fact that after the final moment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there arises another distinct wisdom for a single moment that is able to know the specific characteristics and distinctions of the four truths.
Although within the path of seeing one also knows the four truths in a single moment, this is merely a general comprehension;

it is not yet an individualized knowledge. Because its purpose is to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), it does not yet perform correct discrimination, nor is it yet capable of grasping the four truths in their particularity.
Regarding the characteristic of differentiation: if one asserts that this wisdom which discerns differentiations is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), why is it called "extremes" (*anta*)?

If one does not call it "extremes," how do the fundamental tenet (*mūlārtha*) and the derivative tenet (*uttarārtha*) differ, given that both are true direct realizations (*abhisamaya*) of the wisdom that discerns differentiations?
The five consciousness-bodies, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, possess both defilement and freedom from defilement.

The commentary states that there are two explanations regarding this: The first explanation holds that they are "free from defilement" because they are induced by preparatory application (*prayoga*) to give rise to the Noble Path;

just as at the time of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), the Noble Path arises, and thus it is called "freedom from defilement. However, they are not capable of actually severing defilement. The second explanation maintains that since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the five consciousnesses is already admitted [to be free from defilement], they are therefore free from defilement.

It is beyond doubt that, when categorized as untainted (*anāsrava*), these are capable of abandoning defilements, for it is established that the consciousness perceiving the Buddha can sever afflictions (*kleśa*).
Nevertheless, when these five consciousnesses arise within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
they possess six bodies of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*) in the realms of form and formlessness.
The commentary states: Within the three realms, it is accepted that all possess form, because subtle sense-faculties and great elements can exist therein.
Thus, the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) possesses the six groups of consciousness; by this principle, one should know that the higher realms also possess the two objects of odor and flavor.

However, because they differ only slightly [from those in the lower realms], they are omitted here. This being so, although those [beings] do not perceive the odors and flavors of their own realm, even though these [objects] are not present...
Since it is taught that the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*) also possess the objects of fragrance and taste, the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would likewise possess all eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

This is not stated here because it is abbreviated; it is implied that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth are also present. Question: If there is indeed form (*rūpa*) in the Formless Realm, why is it called the "Formless Realm"?
Answer: It is called the "Formless Realm" because it possesses subtle form and lacks coarse form. Question: In the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), form is not coarse; should this not also be the case?
Question: It is called the "Formless Realm" (ārūpyadhātu). Answer: Although form (*rūpa*) in the Formless Realm is superior to that of the Desire Realm, it is inferior to [the state of] formlessness;

thus, while it can only be called the "Realm of Form," it cannot receive the name "Formless. Question: Since untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*) is superior to the form of the Formless Realm, it should be called "Formless.
Answer: Because it is not the fruit of karma and does not fall within the realms (*dhātu*), although it is extremely subtle, it cannot be said to be non-existent.

Because of form (*rūpa*), one falls into the realm of form; therein, that which possesses extremely subtle form and lacks coarse form is called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It is not because of the absence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and so forth that it receives the name "formless.
The five kinds of material sense-faculties have the physical mass of flesh as their substance.
The commentary states: The Sūtras say that the eye is "derived from the primary elements" (mahābhūtaja) and so forth, up to "the individual nature of solidity and the category of the solid.

From this, we know that the five material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya), such as the eye, all have a mass of flesh (māṃsapiṇḍa) as their substance; there is no separate translucent matter (prasāda-rūpa).
Because non-translucent matter cannot perceive objects, the text subsequently states: [the faculty perceives by means of the translucent matter].
The eye does not see forms, the ear does not hear sounds, the nose does not smell odors, the tongue does not taste flavors, and the body does not perceive tangibles.

[The author] states: Since the substance of the sense organs (*indriya*) is not pure matter (*rūpa*), how could they see forms and so forth? Therefore, it is consciousness (*vijñāna*) that is able to cognize; the sense organs themselves possess no such capacity.
In the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), there is the utterance of speech, as well as the disciplining of the mind and the mental engagement with conflict (*raṇa-manasikāra*).

The commentary states: the mind in the state of meditative equipoise does not exclusively take the object of concentration as its focus; therefore, within a single moment of mind, multiple objects can be apprehended.

Since it is admitted that one utters speech, [the mind] also takes vocal karma as its object. However, no instance has been seen where it is admitted that one performs bodily karma while in a state of meditative concentration.
When this concentration relies on movement, because the mind follows that movement, it would necessarily become distracted; therefore, one must tame the mind.
This means that when the mind takes the object of concentration as its focus, the mind becomes supple and compliant, which is called "taming.
This clarifies that speech arises from a mind established in concentration, not from a distracted mind; it is precisely this tamed, concentrated mind that [gives rise to speech].

Within [the mind] there is also that which is "with contention" (*saraṇa*). Because it is distracted toward external objects and is rigid rather than perfectly disciplined, it is called "with contention.
"Contention" (*raṇa*) is a synonym for "defect" (*doṣa*). A mind that takes external objects as its object is termed "contending attention" (*raṇamanasikāra*).

Herein, the meaning is intended to show that even within a state of single-minded concentration (*ekāgra-citta*), there may arise speech; and that while the mind is one-pointed, it may take two objects, such that within a concentrated mind, one also grasps at distraction.
Regarding the object, there is one mind with two conditions; at the time of this preparatory application (*prayoga*), it takes only the meditative object as its condition.

Subsequently, when many moments continue in a state of equipoise (*samāhita-citta*), even if it subsequently conditions other objects, it does not lose the previous object. Although it may also condition distracted states, it is still called a "concentrated mind" (*samāhita-citta*).

Furthermore, it cannot be understood that within a single concentrated mind, the arising of defiled consciousness is permitted—this is what is termed "contentious attention" (*raṇa-manasikāra*). If [it were]...
Because a defiled mind is contrary to a pure one, if there were another distinct consciousness, it would contradict the fundamental tenet that cognitions do not arise simultaneously;
otherwise, it would conflict with the final tenet which asserts that all consciousnesses can coexist.
"Having completed what was to be done, there is no further capacity for receiving dharmas.

The commentary states: "Having completed what was to be done" refers to those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa). They have no further capacity for receiving dharmas because they do not grasp at the differentiated characteristics of objects.
When they take objects as their cognitive focus, they merely know them as phenomena produced by causes and conditions, neither clinging to nor grasping them.
The meaning of "the absence of grasping because there is no room for the perception of distinctions in objects" is as follows:

schools such as the Sarvāstivāda maintain that even those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) still grasp at distinctions in objects. Regarding the old interpretation stating there are "two locations"—first, the location of attachment, and second, the location of rebirth—the precise significance of this sequence of cause and effect remains unclear.
The mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of all stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) are able to cognize their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
[Commentary: All stream-enterers know for themselves that they have realized the fruit of stream-entry; they do not depend on seeking out the words of others or teachings before they understand it.
Furthermore, it is said that those minds and so forth, in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), are able to cognize their own intrinsic nature, distinguishing them from other schools.
Although all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can understand their own nature, the latter three fruits and so forth are all likewise;
however, because ordinary beings have not yet attained clear realization, the first fruit of the noble ones (*ārya-phala*) is cited.
There are arhats who, being enticed by others, still possess ignorance and even doubt, and are led to awakening and entry by others.
The Way arises from sound.
[The commentary] states: Mahādeva divided the Mahāsāṃghika school, and his descendants have now presented five points;
their essential meaning is the same as before, and since the textual evidence establishes the tenets, there is no need for further elaboration.

"Suffering can induce the Path. [The author] explains: "Suffering" refers to the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā-vedanā*), which is capable of inducing the Noble Path immediately thereafter. [Question: What kind of Path does it induce? [Answer: It induces the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This is because [the Path of Seeing] cannot arise prior to the Path of Cultivation; otherwise, it would contradict the principle of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*). Necessarily...
It should be so. Harsh words can provide assistance.
The commentary states: that frequent expressions of suffering, weariness, and detachment from the world can also assist in fulfilling what is to be accomplished through the Noble Path.
Wisdom serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) that can extinguish all suffering and can also induce happiness.

[The commentary] states: This means that ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth cannot serve as the preparatory application to extinguish all suffering, nor can they induce the supreme fruits of happiness—namely, *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*; only wisdom can do so.
Suffering is also nutriment.
The commentary states: because sentient beings in the hells maintain their life-span even when receiving hot iron balls, suffering is nutriment.
Thus, it is generally accepted that the three types of sensation are called nutriment.
One may also dwell for a long time in the eighth stage.
The commentary states: Counting from the Arhat as the first, one arrives at the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-pratipannaka) as the eighth.
According to the intention of this school, when the householder Sudatta once offered a meal to the Saṃgha, [he saw] in the sky...
A deity spoke, saying: "This one is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry; this one has attained the fruit of stream-entry," and so forth, as explained at length.
Since it is granted that a candidate for the first fruit receives offerings of food, it is clearly known that one may also emerge from the contemplation of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Although one knows that by contemplating the principle of the Four Noble Truths with a single mind, one severs the afflictions, the afflictions are not yet exhausted; nevertheless, one may emerge from contemplation, just as one previously contemplated the principle of the four true truths of the desire realm.

Having severed the afflictions of the desire realm and emerged from meditative absorption, [the practitioner] receives the offering of Sudatta; subsequently, upon re-entering [absorption], they simultaneously sever the [afflictions] of the higher realms.

Therefore, one who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) may also remain [in that state] for a long time. It is not said that they must undergo further rebirths to attain the fruit of the candidate.

According to the traditional explanation, the first fruit consists of at most seven births; this is based on the desire realm alone. However, in each of the higher realms, there is likewise only one birth.

The same applies to those who have entered the path (*pratipannaka*); therefore, it is possible for them to undergo further births. This principle has not yet been fully detailed, as it does not specify how many births one who has first entered the path must pass through.
Furthermore, it can be said that even those at the stage of the "nature-ground" (*gotrabhūmi*) are subject to falling back from their attainments.
The commentary states: Regarding the "dharmas of the stage of nature" (*gotrabhūmi-dharma*), these are the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).

As stated in the third fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā*, this teaching holds that from the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up to the supreme mundane dharmas, there is retrogression (*parihāṇi*).

Because the supreme mundane dharmas involve a succession of multiple moments, there is retrogression; it is not the case that at the time of attaining the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), one also retrogresses accordingly. This is what is meant here.
Because there is falling back when one has regressed from the stage of abiding in the nature of the ground prior to attaining the first fruit;
thus, while there is the possibility of regression for a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), there is no possibility of regression for an arhat.

The commentary states: "The first fruit merely eliminates all afflictions through a single path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that is untainted (*anāsrava*), yet it does not yet involve concurrent cultivation."

Since the delusions within their bodies are not yet exhausted, the noble dharmas they have cultivated are not yet perfected, and the noble path they have attained is not yet firm, it is possible for them to fall away from it.
How could there be such falling away from the fourth fruit? This would contradict the principle [of its security]. Question:
Regarding the second and third fruits, is there falling away or no falling away? Answer: Just as with the first fruit, there is indeed falling away from them as well.
Because its principle is not subject to doubt, the treatise does not mention it.
There is no mundane right view and no mundane faculty of faith.
The commentary states: although mundane wisdom and faith exist, because their substance lacks superior efficacy, they are not designated as "faculties" (*indriya*); however—

Untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) abandons the afflictions and realizes cessation; the untainted faculty of faith (*anāsrava-śraddhendriya*) attains verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding the precepts, the Buddha, and the Dharma.

Because it possesses this superior function, it is designated as a "faculty" (*indriya*). Question: Do the mundane factors conducive to enlightenment (*laukika-bodhipakṣa*) also possess the five faculties?

Answer: No. It is essential that they be at the untainted stage to be called "faculties. However, in the untainted state, they are specifically designated as "faculties" based on their distinct functions.
The power [of these factors] is equal to the principle and not contradictory to it.
There are no indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas.
The commentary states: because the objects of perception differ for each individual, the karmic results induced by wholesome and unwholesome actions are each distinct; therefore, they are wholesome.

Since they are designated as "wholesome" when they induce wholesome results and "unwholesome" when they induce unwholesome results, there are no neutral (avyākṛta) afflictions in the two higher realms. What is the nature of these [afflictions]?

The answer is: they are exclusively unwholesome. Regarding the two types of transformation minds (*nirmāṇacitta*), what is their nature? The answer is: they are subsumed under the category of the wholesome.
When entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one may be said to sever all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The commentary states: "Fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*) are of one substance but different names; 'fetter' has the meaning of binding.

Since noble persons (*ārya*) no longer possess the sense of being disturbed by afflictions, yet they still possess them [in a latent form] upon entering the noble state, one may say that all fetters are severed when entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)."
Because they are never bound within the cycle of birth and death, it is logically possible for them to possess various afflictions;
those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer may commit all manner of evil deeds, with the sole exception of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).

The commentary states: Stream-enterers (srotāpanna) may still commit the ten paths of unwholesome action, provided they exclude the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), because those are of the utmost gravity.

Since it is difficult to distinguish between ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*) based on this alone, one might ask: "How can those who have attained the first fruit possess indestructible faith (*akopya-prasāda*) yet still commit the ten unwholesome actions, which would seem to constitute a breach of their precepts?

The answer is that there is no contradiction; for while they may enter meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) and realize the purities (*prasāda*), they may still engage in unwholesome conduct upon emerging from that observation.

Question: If that were so, one should enter meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) without doubt regarding the Three Jewels, yet upon emerging from observation one doubts again. Answer: The doubt arises because one is confused about the principle.

In the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), the ten paths of unwholesome action (*akuśala-karmapatha*) are entirely absent; however, their manifestations are subtle, and thus they still exist in the stage of the first fruit.
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are all of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The commentary states: All words uttered by the Buddha turn the wheel of Dharma and accord with the True Dharma; therefore, they are called "definitive meaning.
This encourages reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning, because what the Buddha taught does not rely on the teachings of non-definitive meaning, such as the paths of outsiders. Thus, the Buddha...
Question: Regarding the statement in the sūtras that one who kills their father and mother is pure—what is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of such a cryptic teaching?
Answer: Because sentient beings are produced through long-standing causes of hatred and attachment, these two fetters are spoken of as "father" and "mother.
Since this accords with correct reasoning, how could it not be of definitive meaning?
There are nine kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The commentary states: "Kinds" refers to categories; there are nine distinct types of unconditioned phenomena.
First, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); third, space (*ākāśa*).
The commentary states: These preceding three types are all one substance; they manifest as distinct states (*avasthā*) rather than being multiple in essence.
The remaining explanations of their names and so forth do not differ from those of other schools.
[1] The Sphere of Infinite Space, [2] the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, [3] the Sphere of Nothingness, and [4] the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.

Regarding the "bases of perception" (*saṃjñā-āyatana*): the commentary states that these four formless bases have as their support a distinct unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state, which is comprised within cessation (*nirodha*).

One must first attain this cessation and rely upon it to be born in those [formless realms]. The subtle five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that serve as the supported [existence] therein are themselves impermanent; thus, [the unconditioned] is the support for these four.
The formless realms (*ārūpya*) are inherently permanent; however, the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) have no separate basis and are subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is because the aggregates (*skandha*) are not extremely subtle, and the elements (*dhātu*) are not extremely superior. Since the mind and its concomitants, which serve as the support, can take objects in higher or lower realms without obstruction, this is not the case for the formless realms.
Because the mind does not take lower realms as its object, there is an obstruction; thus, there must be a distinct unconditioned entity that serves as their basis.

Because it is based on its locus (*āśraya*), it cannot be used as a precedent. However, "emptiness" refers to the contemplation of emptiness; it is not that all coarse matter is entirely absent, but rather that it is called "empty" because coarse matter is not present.

The explanations for the remaining terms and so forth should all follow the standard interpretations. Their designations are established in accordance with the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which they depend.
The nature of the eight factors of dependent origination and the nature of the nine factors of the noble path.

The commentary states: Regarding the nature of the factors of dependent origination, it means that within the cycle of birth and death, phenomena are fixed such that volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth definitely arise only after ignorance (*avidyā*), and ignorance and so forth definitely exist prior to volitional formations and so forth.
This principle is of a single nature, eternally constant, and determinate; thus, ignorance and the other factors [are established].
The principle that the twelve links of dependent origination are comprised within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the principle that all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
the principle that their nature is to be free from defilement and thus eternal and unitary, and the principle that their eightfold distinctions are inherently subject to arising and ceasing—

these are established as the definitive characteristics of nature because they resolve doubts regarding the distinct principles governing cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and the noble path (*āryamārga*). Thus, their nature and characteristics are determined.
Although it is a settled principle of all noble truths that death must necessarily arise from ignorance and that the noble path must necessarily lead to liberation from suffering and so forth,
here we cite the most prominent factors and specifically mention the Eightfold Path.
The nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, yet it is said to be impure when it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The commentary states: Since beginningless time, the essence of the mind has been inherently pure; however, because it arises with afflictions and is thus defiled, it is called "defiled.

These afflictions are not the beginningless, fundamental nature of the mind, and therefore they are designated as "adventitious" (*āgantuka*). Question: Sentient beings have possessed minds since beginningless time—how is this described?

Question: Since the nature of the mind is pure and the mind is fundamentally undefiled, is it not the case that it is inherently noble (*ārya*)? Answer: Sentient beings have no beginning, and the nature of their minds is likewise so;

because as long as there is a mind, it is defiled, it is therefore not noble. Question: If the mind is defiled as long as it exists, why do you now say that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) and that defilement is adventitious (*āgantuka*)?
Is it not the case that guest and host are identical? Answer: It is because at the time of subsequent cultivation on the path, the defilements...
Because only the purity of intrinsic nature remains when [the defilements] have been separated and extinguished, the defilements are called "adventitious.
The *anuśayas* (latent dispositions) are neither mind (*citta*) nor mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), and they lack an object of perception (*ālambana*).
The commentary states: "The *anuśayas* are precisely greed and so forth; these *anuśayas* are also of ten kinds, and they arise even during the state of being without mind (*acittaka-avasthā*)."

The designation of "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth during states such as wholesome [minds] occurs solely because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are constantly present within the body.

If these were mental factors (*caitta*), then in states such as the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), they would have to be absent; yet, since there are no afflictions in those states, they cannot be mental factors. Furthermore, because they are not associated with the mind or its factors, they lack an objective referent (*ālambana*);
for that which possesses an objective referent must necessarily be a mental factor.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) differ from the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and the outbursts differ from the latent dispositions; it should be stated that the latent dispositions are dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*), whereas the outbursts are associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*).

The commentary states: "Outbursts" refers to the various manifest afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth; the latent dispositions and these [outbursts] differ in their essential nature. As for the outbursts...
Since these latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the mind cannot be present in a state of association, they are subsumed under the category of non-associated [dispositions]. Furthermore,
those of the past and future do not possess a real substantial entity.

The commentary states: That which currently possesses both essence and function may be termed "substantially existent. Since past and future lack such essence and function, they are neither substantially existent.
They are designated as "past" and "future" because they have existed or will exist.
All phenomena, in their fundamental state, are neither objects of knowledge nor objects of cognition; rather, they are that which is thoroughly realized.

The commentary states: The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is that which is observed by the mind; it is not something known by ordinary conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), nor is it cognized by impure, distracted consciousness.
It must be thoroughly realized by those who have attained at least a portion of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and those who perceive the ultimate truth.
The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth are known specifically by those who have fully exhausted the path for severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Question: Since mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth are objects known by the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), why is it said that the unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is not an object of knowledge?
Who knows it, and how is it known? Answer: Its substance is subtle; only those who have attained the Truth (*tattva*) and the like can know it.

Therefore, it is also not [ordinarily] an object of knowledge. Question: Since the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) is also known by the cognition of others' minds, it should not be an object of knowledge.

[Question: It is also not something that can be cognized; why then is it not so stated? [Answer: The substance of the mind (*citta*) is coarse and is indeed an object of cognition. However, the mental factors (*caitta*), being subtle in nature, differ from the mind.

Because it would be difficult [to establish them otherwise] apart from the mind, they possess a distinct substance. For this reason, they are not objects of cognition [in that specific sense]. [Question:

Worldly knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) takes the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth as its objects, while scattered consciousness (*vikṣiptavijñāna*) takes other minds and mental factors as its objects. Is this object...?

Question: What is the answer to this? It is merely that the mind of inference (*anumāna*) takes as its object a semblance of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), not the actual sphere of phenomena. Question:
If it is not the actual [sphere], in which sphere is it included? Answer: Just as when one takes the past or future as an object, what sphere does their substance belong to?

Now, although taking mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth as objects is also included within the sphere of phenomena, it is not the actual sphere of phenomena, because it is not an object of direct knowledge (*vijñeya*).

There is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at all. The commentary states: Even if death occurs here and birth occurs there across a great distance of time or space, since there is no intervening interval between the preceding cessation and the subsequent arising, we do not say that there is a separate intermediate state. [Question: Regarding the *Saptabhava-sūtra* and other texts, what is this intermediate state? [Answer: The commentary states: Even if death occurs here and birth occurs there across a great distance of time or space, since there is no intervening interval between the preceding cessation and the subsequent arising, we do not say that there is a separate intermediate state. [Question: Regarding the *Saptabhava-sūtra* and other texts, what is this intermediate state? [Answer: It is the state of existence that arises immediately after death and before rebirth. Because it is subtle and difficult to perceive, it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Seven Existences*. Furthermore, because it is included within the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*), it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Five Aggregates*. Because it is included within the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Twelve Bases*. Because it is included within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Eighteen Elements*. Because it is included within the four nutriments (*catvāra āhārāḥ*), it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Four Nutriments*. Because it is included within the three realms (*tridhātu*), it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Three Realms*. Because it is included within the two truths (*dve satye*), it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Two Truths*. Because it is included within the one dharma (*ekadharma*), it is not mentioned in the *Sūtra on the One Dharma*. The commentary states: The first two phrases reveal that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of each of the four truths (*catuḥsatya*) are distinct; the latter two phrases reveal that the wisdoms (*jñāna*) regarding the four truths each observe their respective characteristics.

Now, it is revealed that in true observation, each truth is observed individually. Question:

Since this is an individual observation, is it an observation by four moments of mind, or is it an observation by sixteen moments of mind? Answer: Because this is what is cultivated during the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), it is [an observation] regarding the objects of focus.

Regarding the Four Truths: in this present school (the Sarvāstivāda), because one contemplates their distinct characteristics through the wisdom of clear observation (*abhisamaya*), it may be called the "contemplation of sixteen moments of mind.

However, according to our own school (the Sautrāntika), it may be called the "contemplation of four moments of mind," since it is stated that one knows the distinctions among all characteristics by means of the wisdom at the limit (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*).

"There is a small portion of phenomena produced by oneself, a small portion of phenomena produced by another, a small portion of phenomena produced by both, and a small portion of phenomena arising from a multitude of conditions.
The commentary states: This generally demonstrates that all phenomena possess functional activity; within these phenomena, there is a small portion produced by oneself.
There are certain phenomena that are produced by the activity of another and not by their own activity; these are called "produced by the activity of another.
This does not mean that there are phenomena within another's body produced by the joint activity of both self and other.
Furthermore, all schools maintain that although there is no real activity, phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions.

this indicates that a small portion of phenomena is produced by their own activity, and does not indicate that these phenomena are produced by a small amount of activity.
There is a time when two minds arise simultaneously.

The commentary states: Originally it was reckoned that the various consciousnesses arise one by one in successive moments; later, however, it was maintained that two minds arise simultaneously because the forces of the sense organ, the object, and mental attention (manasikāra) arise together.
The Path and the afflictions each manifest simultaneously.
The commentary states: Although it was previously accepted that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) exist separately, it was not stated that they coexist in the same moment as the Path.
Now, since it is accepted that the latent dispositions are ever-present, when the Noble Path arises, they manifest simultaneously with it, just as the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions does.
Because they coexist, it is now stated that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Karma and its maturation (*vipāka*) can function simultaneously.
The commentary states: since there is no past karma and fruit at different times, as long as the karma has not yet been exhausted, the present fruit exists constantly.

Since it has already manifested and matured, its fruit is experienced simultaneously with the karma; yet, even if the karma is exhausted, it need not belong to the same temporal period. According to other schools, they certainly do not belong to the same period.
It is like a seed becoming a sprout.

The commentary states: It is accepted that form (rūpa) undergoes arising and ceasing only over a period of time; therefore, the substance of the seed transforms directly into the sprout, rather than the sprout arising only at the moment the seed ceases.
In other schools, it is held that the seed must cease before the sprout is produced. This is what distinguishes the present position, which is now being set forth.

The sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) possess the quality of transformation (*pariṇāma*), whereas the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) lack this quality of transformation.
The commentary states: Because material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) arise and perish over a long duration, it is admitted that the substance of milk transforms into curd;

however, because the mind and mental factors arise and perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*), the preceding state does not transform into the succeeding phenomenon. This school maintains such a view regarding the faculties.
Because it is of the nature of a mass of flesh, the great elements all undergo transformation, whereas the mind and its associates do not.
The mind pervades the body.

The commentary states: because the subtle mental consciousness (manovijñāna) dwells pervasively throughout the body, one is able to perceive and experience sensation whether the hand, the thorn, or the foot is touched.

Knowing that the subtle mental consciousness dwells pervasively throughout the body and cannot be sequentially awakened in a single moment, one definitively knows that the subtle mind dwells pervasively within the body;
the mind can be observed to contract or expand according to its dependence on objects.

The commentary states: For all schools, the bases and objects of consciousness and so forth have already been determined; that is, the large and small objects, as well as the large and small faculties, have been fixed from beginningless time.

These consciousnesses are invariably and exclusively attributed [to their respective faculties]; it is not the case that a consciousness based on a small faculty could also depend on a large faculty, nor that a consciousness based on a large faculty could also depend on a small faculty.
The same applies to their objects; therefore, they are all predetermined from the outset. This means:
Because the specific conditions such as blue and so forth, as well as the general consciousnesses and so forth, are all predetermined beforehand, this school’s position is incorrect.
There is no predetermined basis or object prior to the fact that consciousness is fixed as belonging to this particular faculty or this particular objective field.

If one relies on a large faculty and perceives a large object, the mind follows the faculty and the object, and thus it is said to "expand" (*śuśu*); "expand" has the meaning of unfolding, which constitutes "greatness. If one relies on...
When the faculty is small and the object is also small, the mind follows along with the faculty and the object and thus "contracts";
"contraction" (juan) carries the meaning of shrinking, which constitutes being small. Here, "basis" (yi) refers to the supporting faculty, while "object" (jing) refers to the perceived object.
Since consciousness has no fixed affiliation, this differs from other schools.

The commentary states: "Sound" refers to vocal sound, which is the very substance of the teaching (*śāsana*).
This teaching of vocal sound is called "supramundane" (*lokottara*) because it can transcend the world and also lead others to give rise to the path of liberation.

That is to say, these five types of teaching sounds—those that express impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*—are necessarily supramundane. Even if one were to depart from these five, [the eightfold path]...
The teachings on the seven factors of enlightenment and so forth are all supramundane; the eightfold path and others that function with these same modes of activity are likewise supramundane.
All other [teachings] should be understood accordingly. That is to say, hearing these five types of teaching is beneficial;

since they accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they are neither of indeterminate meaning (*neyārtha*) nor taught as skillful means (*upāya*). They are certainly supramundane. The treatise states this solely because of the single reality.
The meaning is that these five are able to lead forth the path of transcendence; therefore, they are supramundane teachings.
Other teachings, even if they were able to lead forth the path of transcendence, are not necessarily so, and thus they are not supramundane.
The remaining utterances of the Tathāgata are worldly teachings.
The commentary states: Since they do not definitively lead one to the path of deliverance, they are now collectively termed "worldly teachings.

Its substance is neither present nor substantially existent. Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, if one asks whether they are conventional or real:
they also possess the sense of being conventional, being accumulations based on supports and conditions; therefore, these too are not real.
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are mutually dependent and combined; they are conventionally designated as 'suffering' (*duḥkha*) and lack the agency of a person (*puruṣa*).

[The commentary] states: This explanation of suffering means that the two types of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) existing in the present are mutually dependent and thus called "suffering";

Regarding the realms: from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), even the inferior untainted states are called suffering because the Peak of Existence itself is called suffering;

It is because when the functional capacity of karma brings about a fruit, its characteristics and activity increase to become a cause of maturation (*vipākahetu*) before it can induce that fruit;

"Because of merit, one attains the Noble Path; the Path cannot be cultivated. The commentary states:
Since it is observed that the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) cannot result in the attainment of the Noble state, one knows that the Noble Path cannot be produced through cultivation.

Rather, it is attained solely through the merit of upholding the precepts, giving, and so forth; at the moment one becomes a Noble One, the fruit of the Noble state is spontaneously realized. Therefore, [the Noble Path] cannot be cultivated.

Through the power of wisdom, one attains the noble state of direct realization (*pratyakṣa*) via the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); if one does not attain the noble state, it is said that one attains direct realization through merit (*puṇya*).
If giving were not to constitute the noble state, then one must explain that the path is attained through cultivation.
