therefore, no great fruit or even small merit can be accomplished. By this principle, it should be understood that giving material objects to the Dharma likewise yields no great fruit—this is the tenet of this school.
As for *stūpa*, this is translated as "high and superior place," referring to the high and superior site where the *śarīra* (relics) are enshrined.
These are the bases.

Regarding the fundamental tenets shared by the Sarvāstivāda school itself: it is held that all phenomena (*dharma*) that exist according to the Sarvāstivādins are subsumed under two categories—namely, name (*nāman*) and form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, the essence (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, whether past or future, is substantially real (*dravyasat*), and all phenomena are included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

All these are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), as well as objects of cognition (*vijñeya*) and objects of thorough penetration (*parijñeya*). They are comprised within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), specifically the notions of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Those who advocate "everything exists" (*sarvāstivāda*) maintain that there are two kinds of "all": first, all phenomena (*dharma*), which refers to the five categories of phenomena.

That is to say, at all times—past, future, and present—the mind, mental factors, matter, formations dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned are each subsumed under "name" and "form" in relation to their respective schools, such that these encompass all phenomena. Matter is called "form" because its characteristics are coarse and prominent, making its essence easy to know.
The four aggregates and the unconditioned have essences that are subtle and hidden, difficult to perceive; thus, their appearance is manifested through "names."
Therefore, it is called "the locus of all phenomena (dharmāyatana), that which is known, cognized, and realized. The intention of this school is as follows:

since the essence and characteristics of the mind and mental factors are similar, and since the mind is already admitted to be a cognition, why are the mental factors not also said to be the locus of phenomena?
Furthermore, it is admitted that conventional knowledge knows them; that contaminated consciousness cognizes them; and that the six supernormal powers realize the true principle.

That which is thoroughly understood by [the masters] as being comprised within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—namely, the phenomena of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence—is not inconsistent with the Sautrāntikas and others, for it is not [merely] the aggregate of formations.

There are three kinds of conditioned entities (*saṃskṛta-vastu*), and there are likewise three kinds of unconditioned entities (*asaṃskṛta-vastu*). Furthermore, the three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) exist as distinct, real entities.
The three truths constitute the conditioned, while one truth constitutes the unconditioned.
The gradual clear realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) of the four noble truths may be entered through either the two samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apranihita*).

One who intends to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is said to be "practicing toward" (*pratipannaka*) the tenth stage during the fifteen moments of mind once they have already entered that state of right determination.
The six moments of mind are said to be "abiding in the fruit.

Regarding the statement that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) have three [characteristics] and so forth: "conditioned" refers to the three time periods; "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*).
Regarding the entry into the state of rightness (*samyaktva-nyāma*): these two [types of entry] pertain to the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Therefore, one enters into the correct nature [of reality] through the inclusion of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and through the inclusion of emptiness, selflessness (*anātman*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Because they include suffering (*duḥkha*) and impermanence (*anitya*), the practice of views relies on emptiness, while the practice of craving relies on wishlessness.
There are two types of the practice of views: first, that in which the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) predominates; second, that in which the view of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*) predominates.

The practice based on the predominance of the view of self relies on the samādhi of emptiness of selflessness (*anātma-śūnyatā-samādhi*); the practice based on the predominance of the view of "mine" [relies on wishlessness].

Based on the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā* samādhi, there are two types of craving for practice: first, when laziness increases, one relies on the suffering of birth and death, thinking, "I must not cling to laziness and negligence for the sake of pleasure";
second, when self-conceit (*asmimāna*) increases, one relies on the *anitya-animitta* samādhi, thinking, "Since all things are without self, do not give rise to self-conceit."

The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) consists of one mind and three grades; the Supreme Mundane Dharma is definitively non-retrogressive. For those who have entered the stream (*srotāpanna*), there is no possibility of retrogression;
for Arhats, there is the possibility of retrogression. It is not the case that all Arhats attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are able to sever sensual desire and ill-will. There are certain non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) who can attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and there are also those among the gods who abide in the Brahma realm.
Regarding the practitioner:

the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) consist of three grades, corresponding to the three vehicles. Among the Śrāvakas, those who fall back from the stage of *dhyāna* (思) are of the lower grade;

those who are "guardians" (*anurakṣa-dharman*), "steadfast" (*sthitākampya*), or "capable of penetration" (*prativedhanādharman*) are of the middle grade; and those who are "immovable" (*akopyadharman*) are of the upper grade. However, this [distinction] applies only to the lower [grades].

In the lower realms, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not established; the same applies to the middle and upper realms. Among the gods, there is also the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*);
engaging in sexual intercourse with women is called non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*). Yet, those dwelling in the heavens are by nature free from such acts, as the Sūtra says:
"A certain bhikṣu was diligent in maintaining the precepts. At night, while washing his feet, there was a foot-rest in the basin, and upon it was a snake."
While circumambulating and dwelling among the bhikṣus, he did not notice his feet being drawn into [the water], and was consequently killed by a crocodile.
He was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, within the Nandana Grove. Among all those born as devas, they are either male or female from birth;
however, once he had been born into this grove, he was unlike the other celestial hosts. Before him stood a goddess who wished to embrace the newly born deva, but he threw her hand away, saying:
"None of you should approach me. The celestial maidens were astonished and said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then ordered them to look into a mirror.
When the newly born deva saw his own reflection, he saw that his head was adorned with a celestial crown and his body was graced with necklaces;
it was not the appearance of one who had previously left the household life. He felt deep remorse and his revulsion toward desire increased even further. The celestial maidens, because of this—"

Having addressed this to Śakra, when Śakra heard it, he personally paid him homage; knowing that [the practitioner] had formerly left the human world to renounce the householder’s life and maintain the precepts, he then escorted him to the Garden of Celestial Immortals.
Thus, one knows that there is the practice of pure conduct (brahmacarya) among the devas.

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are obtainable within seven attainments (*samāpatti*), but not in others. Not all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
One may enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and even attain the fruit of arhatship without relying on the dhyānas;

however, while one may realize the fruit of arhatship by relying on a body in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one cannot enter the state of right determination from those states.
Based on a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is not only able to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) but can also realize the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding the seven meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that possess the factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), these consist of the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*). For brevity, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*) are not mentioned;
however, this is because certain schools maintain that the factor of enlightenment exists specifically in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the desire realm.
In Uttarakuru, there are none who have become free from passion; the Noble Ones are not born there, nor in the Heaven of Non-perception.

The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are not necessarily attained gradually; however, if one has previously entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one may realize the fruit of once-returner or non-returner by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
In Uttarakuru, there are none who become free from defilement, because it consists purely of pleasure and lacks any suffering that could be loathed;
whereas among the six classes of gods, since suffering still exists, they are able to become free from defilement.
It can be said that the four foundations of mindfulness encompass all phenomena, for all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are mental factors (*caitta*) and are associated with the mind.
All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have an associated object of perception are subsumed under the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), but not all fetters are subsumed under the latent dispositions.
The nature of the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-anga*) is necessarily conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have three aspects: first, their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), which is wisdom (prajñā); second, their objects (ālambana), which are all phenomena (sarvadharma);

and third, their retinue (parivāra), which consists of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha). Regarding the fetters (paryavasthāna), there are those that are not underlying tendencies (anuśaya), while the underlying tendencies themselves consist of only seven fetters.
These fetters pervade all afflictions; all afflictions of the three periods of time are fetters, unlike the eighteen fetters and so forth.
There are also members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that continue to function even in an Arhat.

Furthermore, regarding those members of dependent origination that follow an Arhat, how many members continue to function? The answer is: ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) do so;

or else, birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) exist in the future [in the case of one who attains Arhatship while still in the intermediate state]. However, if one attains the fruit of Arhatship within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), these [latter] members certainly do not exist.

This branch of birth (*jāti-aṅga*) allows for the possibility of birth; however, if the fruit is not obtained within the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*), it is because [that moment] is but a single thought-instant.

Within the branch of feeling (*vedanā-aṅga*), the fruit is likewise definitely obtained and does not persist. Regarding the three branches of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and contact (*sparśa*), some say that the fruit is also obtained therein.
Having previously been cultivated, when one has now reached the stage of name-and-form, consciousness may arise.

If one were to say that because of the Noble Path, one enters Nirvāṇa within the three links of name-and-form, the six sense bases, and contact— namely, attaining Nirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*),

with exertion (*sābhisamskāra*), or without exertion (*anabhisamskāra*)— it would mean that these three links of name-and-form, the six sense bases, and contact are still not clearly manifest as roots. In such a case,
not only would it be impossible to give rise to the Noble Path or attain the fruit, but [the attainment] would exist only within the links of feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

The middle section consists of three types of *prajñā*. According to the former explanation, these correspond to four members; according to the latter explanation following the Arhat, they correspond to one member.

As for their function: those that have already attained the fruit are subsumed under the "completed" (*niṣpanna*) members, while those that have not yet attained the fruit are subsumed under the "incomplete" (*aniṣpanna*) members.
There is no difference in the members themselves; they follow the transformation of the Aśaikṣa.

There are Arhats who increase meritorious karma; these exist only within the realms of desire and form. Their intermediate state (antarābhava) possesses the five groups of consciousness, such as visual consciousness, which are associated with defilement and lack detachment.
They grasp only specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and are devoid of conceptual discrimination (nirvikalpa).
There are Arhats who increase their meritorious karma by further creating new merit and accomplishing wholesome qualities that constitute a portion of merit;

therefore, the five consciousnesses grasp only their own intrinsic nature and are devoid of discrimination. This is discussed in terms of the sense bases (*āyatana*). The *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā* does not permit this [position], nor is there any definitive authority [for it].
[The five consciousnesses] are devoid of discrimination, lacking both calculation (*abhinirūpaṇa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa*).
The entities of mind and mental factors are each substantially real. Mind and mental factors necessarily possess objects of perception (*ālambana*).

Their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) do not associate with their own intrinsic natures, nor does mind associate with mind. There is mundane right view and there is the mundane faculty of faith. There are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas.
Arhats also possess dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). Arhats [possess these].
All [Arhats] have attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), yet not all are able to manifest it; there are Arhats who still experience the results of past karma.
There are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling in a virtuous mind who die while remaining in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), yet they certainly do not pass away from that state.

The liberation of the Buddha and that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are no different, yet the noble paths of the three vehicles each have their own distinctions. The Buddha’s compassion and other virtues do not take sentient beings as their objective support (*ālambana*).

One who clings to the existence of sentient beings cannot attain liberation; it should be said that such a person is still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) have not been severed.

As long as one has not yet entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and has not transcended the stage of an ordinary being, one is merely designated as a "sentient being" based on the continuity of the present appropriated aggregates.
It is with reference to this [continuity] that it is conventionally taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Because for all those who have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the dharmas of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and freedom from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*) are naturally matured, they attain liberation simultaneously with the intermediate and the fundamental [stages];
there is no distinction between the two vehicles (*yāna*) other than the severance of defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*) and the attainment of undefiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
There is no principle of attaining liberation [for them]. Out of the Buddha’s compassion, he does not take sentient beings as an object; for sentient beings do not truly exist.
Because they are conditioned solely by phenomena (*dharma*), there is certainly no phenomenon whatsoever that can transition from a previous life to a subsequent life;

there is only the conventional designation of a *pudgala* (person), which speaks of "transmigration," "living," and "the inclusion of formations. Thus, when the aggregates (*skandha*) have ceased without remainder, there is no transformation, and there is supramundane existence.

In the state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there are also instances that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and wholesome (*kuśala*), which possess causes and are characterized by equipoise (*samāhita*). Within this state, there is no utterance of speech;
rather, it is the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) that constitutes the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), not the mere words of the Tathāgata, all of which serve to turn the Wheel of Dharma.

It is certain that there is not even the slightest phenomenon (*dharma*) capable of passing from a previous life to a subsequent one, because a self (*ātman*) does not exist. If one speaks of a "conventional self" (*prajñapti-ātman*), it may undergo transition;
however, since phenomena (*dharma*) are comprised within the activity of the present moment and perish without remainder as soon as they arise, they do not move on to a subsequent life.
Not a single real phenomenon transforms and reaches a subsequent life, for the prior real self has no transition, and the present phenomenon has none either.
In reality, there is no transformation; [this teaching] refutes all substantial selves and phenomena.
It is not that a single voice of the Buddha can express all dharmas.
Although a single voice of the Buddha expresses all dharmas, while it teaches that all dharmas are without self, it cannot express this in a single thought-moment.
□ Because it is without self, it is like the contemplation of non-self; this system does not take itself as its own object because it defines "self" [only] by way of designation.

Furthermore, the Blessed One also has speech that does not accord with the literal meaning, for not all sūtras spoken by the Buddha are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), as the Buddha himself stated.

All such *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras belong to the category of those whose primary meaning is shared with one's own school (*mūla-nikāya*) while their secondary meaning differs from it; such instances are infinite.

The Buddha’s speech that does not accord with reality (*ayathārtha-vāk*) is established as being of two kinds: first, that which has a purposeful intent (*prayojana*), such as when he spoke of "the falling of rain" in response to a formal inquiry—this has no practical purpose;

second, that which has a specific meaning (*artha*), namely the principle of the actual nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which refers to skillful means (*upāya*) that do not correspond [to the literal sense].
Substantial dharmas refer to such acts as killing one's father or mother.
According to the fundamental tenets shared by the Haimavata school, bodhisattvas are still ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

The Haimavatas maintain that because bodhisattvas are ordinary worldlings, they are identical to the Sarvāstivādins regarding the [requirement of] three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas or one hundred kalpas.
Both are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
However, when a Bodhisattva enters the womb, he does not give rise to craving or attachment.
Because he does not give rise to craving or attachment, it is explained that he acts for the benefit of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); thus, one knows that he undergoes birth intentionally.
There is no craving.
There are no non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who can attain the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).

Because they rely on false teachings, there is no principle for attaining these powers among non-Buddhists; even if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) within [the Buddhist fold] were to rely [on them], [they would not attain them].
Because it is the internal teaching, there is the attainment of penetrating the principle;
furthermore, there are no practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya) dwelling among the gods,
nor are there any practitioners of the holy life dwelling among the gods who possess celestial female consorts and all other superior sensory pleasures, even if they were to be born there.
This refers to those who do not abide in the holy life (*brahmacarya*). There are Arhats who, being led by others, still possess ignorance and doubt;
they enter the path through the voice of another, and their various attachments are for the most part the same as those of the Sarvāstivādins.
There were five matters, such as an Arhat being led astray by others, concerning which the Sthavira school originally contended with the Mahāsāṃghika;
this was the reason for their schism. Now, what contradiction to that original intent is there in establishing these [five points] again?
When they first contended with the Mahāsāṃghika, these points had not yet been established. It was only when the three hundred years were complete that they were accepted by the Sarvāstivādins.
In their debates, they claimed that the Sarvāstivādins’ own fundamental tenet was the existence of the five categories (*pañcavastu*).

However, the former disciples of the Sthaviras lost their original tenets and subsequently established these five categories themselves. Thus we know that as time passed and years accumulated, the sages vanished and ordinary people arose;
since the new differs from the old, what is there to wonder at?
The fundamental tenet shared by the Vātsīputrīya school is that the *pudgala* is neither identical to the aggregates (*skandha*) nor distinct from them.

The Vātsīputrīyas maintain that the *pudgala* is not identical to the aggregates nor separate from them; they assert that there is a real self that is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet it is neither identical to nor distinct from the aggregates. When the Buddha taught "no-self" (*anātman*), he meant only that there is no [self] identical to the aggregates.
The self as conceived by non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*)—whether as distinct from the aggregates or not—is entirely non-existent; it is neither non-existent nor inexpressible.
Since this self cannot be said to be either identical to or distinct from the aggregates, its dimensions, such as size or magnitude, likewise cannot be described;
even until the attainment of Buddhahood, this self remains eternally present.

Names are provisionally designated based upon the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). Regarding what is called a "name provisionally designated based upon the aggregates, bases, and elements": it means that the self is neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates, bases, and elements;
likewise, when the world speaks of "form is the self" up to "phenomena (dharma) are the self," these are merely provisional designations based upon the aggregates and so forth.
If one posits this "self" (ātman), that self is in reality not the aggregates (skandha) and so forth.
Conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) both abide for a duration and also perish momentarily.
That conditioned phenomena both abide for a duration and perish momentarily is precisely the tenet of the Saṃmitīya school derived from this [tradition].
The arising of mind and mental factors, like the flame of a lamp or the sound of a bell, ceases moment by moment;

yet within material phenomena, such as the earth, which endures for kalpas, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth all grow together with it, even though they likewise possess arising and ceasing.
If all phenomena were devoid of a *pudgala*, they could not transition from a previous life to a subsequent one;
it is by means of a *pudgala* that one can speak of such transmigration.
Regarding the phrase "if all phenomena were devoid," the intended meaning here is that there is no transmigration of phenomena to be spoken of, as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has ceased.
At that time, the phenomena (dharma) also perish accordingly; however, because the self does not perish, it is able to proceed from a previous life to a subsequent life.
Thus, one may say that phenomena do not depart from the self and that there is a transmigration.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who are able to attain the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who have attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and can perceive this through direct observation because it is acquired through cultivation.

The five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are neither defiled nor free from defilement; thus, when one severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation, this is called "freedom from desire" (*vītarāga*), but not [freedom from desire] regarding those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).

The five consciousnesses are neither defiled nor free from defilement; they are merely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), entirely devoid of good or evil because they lack conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).
Where there is conceptual discrimination, there is good or evil. As for the statement "if one abandons the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation" and so forth:

this is because the afflictions of cultivation are exclusively deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*) and do not obstruct the principle (*tattva*); since the six types of mundane cultivation (*bhāvanā*) are not a realization of the principle, [they cannot serve as the antidote].

Only those [afflictions] abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are suppressed; those abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) arise from delusion regarding the principles [of reality], and thus can only be permanently severed when the principles are seen.

This applies to all six classes of afflictions among both ordinary beings and noble ones. The same holds true for those separated from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth; here, however, only the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is cited by way of illustration.

The characteristics of "patience" (kṣānti) are termed the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma), which are called "entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth" (samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti).
These characteristics of patience and the supreme mundane dharmas first contemplate the Four Noble Truths; because they generally accept them, they are termed "patience.

They also contemplate the Four Noble Truths, and because they [contemplate] the essential nature (svabhāva) expressed by those truths, they are termed the "characteristics of the supreme mundane dharmas. This may be accepted.
Knowing that these roots are what is recited as the fundamental [teaching], it is said that there are only these four as the roots of goodness.

Once one has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), the twelve moments of mind are called "practicing for the goal" (*pratipannaka*), while the thirteenth moment of mind is called "abiding in the fruit" (*phalastha*).

Regarding those who have already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through the twelve moments of mind and so forth: herein, there are three distinct moments of mind regarding the Truths.

First, the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma of suffering), which contemplates the suffering of the desire realm; second, the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma of suffering), after which one contemplates the afflictions of the truth of suffering in the desire realm—whether they are abandoned or not yet abandoned—since afflictions of the higher realms still remain; and third, the *duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of suffering), which again contemplates their abandonment and so forth.
One then combines the contemplation of suffering in the form and formless realms; because the Truth of Suffering is exhausted across all three realms, one no longer contemplates them separately.

Thus, the twelfth mind is combined into the thirteenth mind. Some say this is the second moment of the Subsequent Knowledge of the Path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), while others say it is the mind that contemplates the Four Truths in their entirety.
Whether through sequential or leap-over attainment of the fruit, the process is the same for sequential attainment.
The second [section] on the three fruits is as usual.
There are many such distinct meanings and reasons for explaining a single verse, due to which different interpretations arise from within this school, resulting in four sub-sects:
namely, the Dharmottarīya, the Bhadrayānīya, the Saṃmatīya, and the Kṣaṇikavāda (or Gokulika). These are the explanations provided by them.
The verse says:
"Once liberated, one falls again; Falling occurs through craving, and one returns. Having attained peace and joy, one delights in what is pleasant;
Following that which is agreeable, one proceeds to the supreme bliss."

Regarding the four distinct interpretations of the meaning of the four sections beginning with "Dharma-samatā" (The Equality of Dharmas), one verse is explained according to the four traditional commentaries:
first, the verse on the Arhat explains "receding" (*parihāṇi*) with the first two lines, "abiding" (*sthiti*) with the next line, and "progressing" (*viśeṣagamana*) with the final line.

Second, regarding the two vehicles' state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the first two lines explain the Arhat, the next line explains the Pratyekabuddha, and the final line [explains the Bodhisattva].

The Buddha Śākyamuni taught that there are six types of persons within the three lower and four higher fruits: first, the person of liberation (*vimukta*), who is the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) because they have attained liberation for the first time;
second, the family-to-family (*kulaṃkula*) person, who is one progressing toward the second fruit; third, the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*); fourth, the one-interval (*ekavīcika*) person;

fifth, the non-returner (*anāgāmin*); and sixth, the arhat. Regarding those already liberated, there are two [types]: first, those who fall back from liberation, and second, those who fall due to craving.
The fourth person is one who returns; the third person corresponds to the third phrase; the fifth person corresponds to the fourth phrase.

Regarding the six types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*)—those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), those who protect themselves (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those who abide (*sthitākampya*), those who are capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*), those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*), and those already liberated (*suvimukta*)—the second person falls further; the first person falls by reason of craving; and the third person returns again.
The fourth person corresponds to the third phrase; the fifth person, to the fourth phrase; and the sixth person [to the first].
Regarding the fundamental tenets shared by the Mahīśāsaka school: the past and future are non-existent (*asat*), while the present and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are existent (*sat*).

Concerning the four noble truths, they are realized simultaneously (*ekakāla-abhisamaya*); at the moment one perceives the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one is able to perceive all the truths. This requires that [the truths] have already been seen.
One who is able to see in this way—namely, that the Mahīśāsaka school holds that the four noble truths are realized simultaneously (ekakṣaṇābhisamaya)—this is the path of seeing (darśanamārga).

It constitutes the contemplation of the universal characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of emptiness and selflessness, entering into a pervasive observation of the four truths as empty and selfless; when one sees the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya), it reaches the point of being able to see in this way.

To see this is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). If one contemplates the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths separately, when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) during the path of cultivation, one is able to contemplate the other three truths simultaneously.

Just as a single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can take the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and ten types of form (*rūpa*) as its object in their entirety and discern them at once, so too is this not the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is only after one has already comprehensively contemplated and seen the principle of the truths that one is able [to proceed].
For this reason, one can see it thus while cultivating the path:
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are neither mind nor mental factors; they are without any object of perception and differ from the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).

The intrinsic nature of the latent dispositions is dissociated from the mind, whereas the intrinsic nature of the outbursts is associated with the mind. Ordinary beings do not abandon desire-attachment or ill-will, yet they lack any external [objects].
The Path can attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

As for the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are not the mind itself, as explained in the standard interpretation. Regarding the statement that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not sever desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) and so forth, the intended meaning is that through the six stages of practice, one does not sever the afflictions but merely suppresses them; this is similar to the Sautrāntika position regarding all afflictions.
The same applies to the two realms. Here, we first cite the case of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and so forth, because these can only be abandoned by means of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
As for the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they cannot be considered such because they are attained through false teachings, such as the ability to fly;
nor can they be considered such when derived from spells, medicines, deities, or spirits, or when it concerns the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), because these are not unimpeded.
Furthermore, for those who dwell as practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) among the gods, there is certainly no intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).

Nor is there an intermediate existence for those dwelling as practitioners of the holy life among the gods because of their abundant pleasure; indeed, there is no such thing as a *gandharva* or similar being [in this context].
These are deities of music who lead [beings to rebirth], as stated in the *Saptabhavasūtra* and explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
There is no Arhat who increases meritorious karma;

there is no Arhat who increases meritorious karma because there are no afflictions that could further increase tainted karma, and because such karma would otherwise transform into the category of merit and so forth.
Thus, [for an Arhat], there is no such karma.
The five consciousnesses are both subject to defilement and free from defilement.
The five consciousnesses are free from defilement because, by taking the vision of the Buddha and so forth as their immediate and proximate cause, they induce the Noble Path;

this is not like the Sarvāstivāda view, which holds that even in the state of immediate succession one cannot [induce it], nor does it mean that the five consciousnesses exist only in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), as some claim.
Upon seeing the Buddha, one immediately attains the noble state and is able to sever the fetters and abandon defilements; yet this is not without conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
All six consciousnesses are associated with vitarka and vicāra.
As for which school asserts that the six consciousnesses possess *vitarka* and *vicāra*, [it is as follows].
There is also the "level-headed" (*samaloṣṭakāñcana*) *pudgala*.

This level-headed *pudgala* is one who, having been born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), is unable to give rise to the lower untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) to attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
When his life is about to end, his fetters (*saṃyojana*) are spontaneously exhausted, and he attains Arhatship.

The Han [master] then entered parinirvāṇa, naming it "Equal Head" (*samaśīrṣa*); this refers to the head of birth-and-death, namely the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the ultimate point beyond which there is no further place of rebirth.
Although he did not give rise to the Noble Path, he nonetheless attained the state of an Aśaikṣa.
There is mundane right view;
there is mundane right view because it does not involve wrong seeking.
There is no mundane faculty of faith.
The mundane faculty of faith and the other mundane faculties are not called "faculties" because they are not firm, are easily shifted or altered, and are not predominant;
nor do they include supramundane meditative concentration.

Regarding those who do not possess supramundane dhyāna: since dhyāna is coarse and most ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and non-Buddhist outsiders are generally able to attain it, it is exclusively contaminated (sāsrava).

This [dhyāna] extends through the six stages of the form realm (rūpadhātu). As for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), how is it that while there is also contaminated dhyāna, there is no separate uncontaminated (anāsrava) dhyāna?
Because it is not called "dhyāna" when it is uncontaminated; therefore, this [text] mentions only the form realm for now.

The realms (dhātu) are fixed; however, when noble ones separately give rise to the untainted (anāsrava) states of the six stages, such as entering the path of seeing (darśanamārga), these are not called dhyāna but are termed samādhi.
Furthermore, there is no untainted vitarka, nor is there any wholesome state that lacks a cause.
Since vitarka (applied thought) is coarse, it is exclusively impure (*sāsrava*); whereas vicāra (sustained thought) is subtle and thus extends to the pure (*anāsrava*).

Among the eight factors of the Path, right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is exclusively impure. While those that assist the path are termed "factors of the path" (*mārgāṅga*), they are not in reality the Path itself.

Furthermore, virtue is not a cause for existence, as it does not serve as the primary cause for inducing saṃsāra; rather, when it assists unwholesome karma, it may lead to rebirth in the realms of humans or devas.
There is also this principle: it is not that the primary cause itself can induce the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
If that is so, what is the nature of the karma of the form and formless realms? It is a subtle unwholesome karma that, by being assisted by wholesome factors, attains such a state;
thus, unwholesome karma extends to the form and formless realms.
The stream-enterer (srotāpanna) may fall away,
because even one who has first attained the path possesses afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
As for the arhats, there are certainly none who fall away.

Because Arhats have no regression and their path is perfected, when it is said that they "regress" and so forth, this refers only to regressing from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the dwelling in happiness in the present life;
there is no regression from the two fruits of reality, as such regression would be like losing a fruit once attained.
The factors of the path are all subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).

Since the factors of the path are all subsumed by the foundations of mindfulness— and because the foundations of mindfulness are defined as the mental concomitants associated with wisdom (prajñā) together with the mind— the foundations of mindfulness thus subsume the factors of the path.

There are nine kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); third, space (*ākāśa*); fourth, the imperturbable (*āniñjya*);

fifth, the suchness of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma-tathatā*); sixth, the suchness of unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma-tathatā*); seventh, the suchness of indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma-tathatā*); eighth, the suchness of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga-tathatā*);
and ninth, the suchness of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-tathatā*).

The three entities of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation), *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation), and *ākāśa* (space) each have one acquisition (*prāpti*), and their objects (*ālambana*) are the same as those of other schools.

Regarding "immovable" (*āniñjya*), it refers only to the abandonment of the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*); it is termed "immovable" because "movement" (*iñjya*) refers to mental distraction (*vikṣepa*). Since this [state] has now been abandoned, it is called "immovable.

As for the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [factors], each of these three entities has one acquisition; however, they are designated by the single term "nature" (*dharmatā*), and all are the objects of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

The arising of these meanings is the same as that of the Great Assembly, yet each possesses its own principle. Now, following the predominant view, we speak only of the dependent origination of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*).

Taking conception in the womb as the beginning and death as the end, the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) all undergo transformation, and the mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) likewise undergo transformation.
From the initial entry into the womb until the final moment of the mind and mental factors, there is also transformation.

What is intended here is that throughout the period from beginning to end, form and so forth undergo transformation—just as milk transforms into curd—and this is because their nature is not subject to momentary arising and ceasing; thus, they possess transformation.
The same applies to the mind and mental factors. However, it is not the case that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) [undergo such transformation].

Regarding momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*): another interpretation holds that although the nature of form and other phenomena is such that they perish moment by moment, they do not possess the distinction of past and future times as the Sarvāstivādins do.
According to the Sarvāstivādins, once a preceding dharma has ceased, a subsequent dharma arises from the future and reaches the present.

What is stated here is that once the preceding dharma has ceased in the present, there is no separate dharma that comes from the future; rather, it is simply through the preceding dharma [that the subsequent one arises].
By the power of the cause, the subsequent dharma is drawn forth; thus, the subsequent dharma is the preceding dharma transformed by acting as its cause.
Although it perishes moment by moment, the meaning of transformation is established.
Because the Buddha is within the Saṃgha, one who gives to the Saṃgha obtains a great fruit, rather than giving specifically to the Buddha alone.
Because the Buddha is within the Saṃgha and is counted among the members of the Saṃgha;
the Buddha and those of the two vehicles all share the same path and the same liberation, and it is taught that all conditioned phenomena are momentary.

Regarding the statement that the Buddha and those of the two vehicles share the same path and the same liberation, the intent of this school is to say that it is not the case that the functional operation of the "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Buddha and the two vehicles is identical. Rather, the path is one;

that is to say, when a śrāvaka eventually becomes a Buddha, the essence of the original path does not change, and its categories are the same. It is simply that by transforming the lower [level], one achieves the middle, and by transforming the middle, one achieves the higher.

Therefore, it was said above that the functions of a single entity in cognizing objects are thus different; however, this does not refer to matters such as abandoning a lower vehicle to attain a higher fruit, or abandoning the inferior to attain the superior.
As for liberation, it is exclusively analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); it severs defiled ignorance and attains the cessation of every moment.
These two types of liberation are the same as previously explained.
It is their fundamental tenet that not even the slightest dharma can transition from a previous life to a subsequent life. Their derivative divergent tenets are as follows:
they assert that the past and future exist substantially; that there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*);

that all dharmas and bases (*āyatana*) are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and objects of cognition (*vijñeya*); and that karma is truly volition (*cetanā*), such that there is no physical or vocal karma.

Since it is certain that not even the slightest phenomenon persists from a prior moment to a subsequent one due to momentary cessation, there is no single real entity that persists from before to after and is associated with vitarka and vicāra.
The association with vitarka and vicāra is explained according to the Sārvastivāda school.
As for the "great earth" abiding for an eon (*kalpa*),
and the fact that this great earth abides for an eon rather than perishing moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-vināśa*), these are explained according to the Saṃmitīya school and others.
The fruit obtained from performing acts of worship at a stūpa is small.
The fruit of worshipping a stūpa is consistently minor, whether it contains relics or not, because there is no one to receive the offering, feel joy, or provide benefit;
this applies equally to images of the Buddha and other such objects.
The intrinsic nature of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) always abides in the present.

Because these latent dispositions, being constantly present, always abide in the present as causes for the arising of all phenomena, they remain uninterrupted throughout the past, future, and present.
The aggregates, bases, and elements are also constantly present.

Regarding the statement that the aggregates, bases, and elements are constantly present: this refers to the fact that the three categories [of seeds] are constantly present and are solely capable of producing all phenomena;
these five dharmas are definitively able to bind and fetter sentient beings, preventing them from emerging from birth and death.
At the conclusion of this school’s doctrine, there is a difference in the interpretation of a single verse; as that verse says:
"Five factors are certainly able to bind; All sufferings arise from them: Namely, ignorance, craving, the five views, And all [karmic] actions."

"All sufferings arise from this; they originate from five factors," namely ignorance and so forth. This enumerates the names of the five factors: first, ignorance, which is the ignorance of the three realms;
second, sensual desire; third, craving for form and the formless; fourth, the four views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and others;
and fifth, various karmas, meaning the three types of karma. As for why only these five are mentioned, it is because all karmas... [text continues].

As previously stated, wholesome states that lack causes constitute meritless and immovable karma; therefore, the function of the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) is preeminent for its role in overcoming the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) which obstruct the principle (*nīti*), while the function of the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) is preeminent for its role in overcoming craving (*tṛṣṇā*) which takes objective phenomena as its object. The five views take internal principles as their objects, and although their modes of activity (*ākāra*) across the various realms are similar, they are collectively termed "the five views.
Craving, however, takes objective phenomena as its object, and its modes of activity differ from those of the views; this is because desire...
Regarding the objects of the realms, because the two upper realms take internal objects as their conditions, craving is divided accordingly.

Although these two types differ in their application—view being associated with the path of seeing and craving with the path of cultivation—they both function as fundamental roots through the path of cultivation; that which is thus fundamental is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, other afflictions are omitted here and not mentioned. Furthermore, ignorance is the member of ignorance, craving is the member of craving, and the five views [are the member of views].

Because the "appropriating" (*upādāna*) link serves as a condition for increasing karma, karma itself constitutes "becoming" (*bhava*). Thus, these five factors are constantly able to bind the seven factors, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), so that they arise.
Furthermore, regarding the two upper realms (*dhātu*), birth does not result from unwholesome karma because unwholesome karma is subtle and weak;

rather, it is through the assistance of wholesome factors that unwholesome karma brings about rebirth in those higher realms. Moreover, there is no wholesome karma that brings about birth in the two upper realms.
Regarding "all actions," this refers to those of body, speech,
and mind. According to the fundamental tenets of the Dharmaguptaka school, although the Buddha is included within the Saṃgha, the fruit of Buddhahood is distinct from that of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the Dharmaguptaka school’s statement that although the Buddha is included within the Saṃgha, when one gives specifically to the Buddha, the mind is free from discrimination;
rather, because one offers to the World-Honored One with a supreme and most excellent, single-minded, equal, and respectful devotion without distinction, one obtains great merit.

If the Buddha were present within the Saṃgha and one were to give to him as well [as part of the group], the mind would instead become lax and arrogant, and furthermore, it would constitute a great conceit.
Furthermore, because one distinguishes between the Buddha as unsurpassed and the Saṃgha as having superiors, the fruit of giving to the Saṃgha is generally small,
whereas the fruit of performing acts of worship at a stūpa is vast.
Regarding the attainment of great fruit through making offerings at a stūpa: because one places the Buddha’s relics within it, seeing this site is like seeing the Buddha himself;
since the mind is thus held in high esteem, one attains great fruit.

Furthermore, as the Buddha himself permitted that making offerings to the relics is no different from making offerings to the Buddha, the fruit is therefore supreme and the Dharma is likewise so—it is not non-existent.
Accepting [such gifts] would indeed lack great fruit, for the Buddha himself permitted the acceptance of such offerings.
Although the liberation of the Buddha and that of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are one and the same, their noble paths differ.
That the liberation of the Buddha and that of the two vehicles are equal can be understood from the text itself.
No non-Buddhists are able to attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
This is because those non-Buddhists who do attain the five supernormal powers teach what is false;

furthermore, "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*) refers to movement that is unobstructed, whereas ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who are not disciples of the Buddha merely practice meditation in a casual manner and cannot attain such powers, as they are unable to remain unobstructed.
The ability to fly or perform feats such as remaining suspended for kalpas and so forth is entirely due to the influence of spells, medicines, spirits, or deities;
it is not genuine supernatural power (*abhijñā*).
The bodies of Arhats are all untainted (*anāsrava*); in other respects, their tenets are largely the same as those of the Mahāsāṃghika school.

That the bodies of Arhats are entirely without outflows (*anāsrava*) has two meanings: first, because they are not the basis for outflows, the aggregates of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not give rise to outflows;

second, because they are not the objects of outflows, even if outflows arise in others [in relation to them], they do not increase—just as although afflictions may arise in relation to the Truths of Cessation and the Path, they do not increase therein. Nevertheless, the aggregates of one beyond training constitute a distinct category.

Because [the fruit] arises and manifests only when one who is still in training (śaikṣa) attains the state of no-more-training (aśaikṣa), even if one should fall away from the state of no-more-training and abide in the stage of training while afflictions arise, these aggregates of training that serve as the basis and object for the arising of those afflictions are not the five aggregates of the body of one in no-more-training;
rather, it is because the aggregates of no-more-training have ceased and the aggregates of training have arisen. However, according to this school...
Although it is not necessarily accepted that there is the sense of falling away (parihāṇi) for those beyond training (aśaikṣa), this interpretation does not contradict reason.
According to the fundamental tenets of the Kāśyapīya school, if a dharma has already been abandoned and fully known, then there is no longer any state of it being un-abandoned or not fully known;
if it has not yet been abandoned or fully known, then such a state exists.
Regarding the statement in the Kāśyapīya school that "if a dharma has already been abandoned and fully known (*parijñāta*), it is then non-existent," "dharma" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

When they have not yet been abandoned, their past existence is termed "having afflictions. Once they have been abandoned through immediate succession and one attains liberation and full knowledge, the substance of those past afflictions is no longer different [from their state as non-existent]; this is unlike the Sarvāstivādins and others, for whom the substance exists independently.
If the fruit of an action has already matured, it does not exist; if the fruit has not yet matured, it exists.

Regarding the phrase "if the fruit of an action has already matured, it does not exist," etc.: since this treats only of action (*karman*), it means that if the fruit has not yet matured, the past action possesses substantial reality (*dravya*);
however, if the fruit has already matured, the action has no substantial reality in the past, for there is only the fruit.
Once a phenomenon has arisen, it ceases moment by moment without depending on its having been abandoned or fully known (*parijñāta*). The commentary explains:
here, [the text] refers only to the past and present, and not the future, because the future lacks substantial existence (*asvabhāva*).

Now, according to the meaning of the text, there is no phenomenon that takes the future as its cause, because the future does not exist. However, since the cause follows and the effect precedes, there is nothing that can take the future as its cause.
Furthermore, because the statement "having already abandoned and known" does not specify a temporal distinction, it is accepted as applying to the future as well; this is logically unobjectionable.
There are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have the past as their cause, but there are no conditioned phenomena that have the future as their cause.
Regarding the statement that "there are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have the past as their cause," this is intended to distinguish [this view] from the Sarvāstivāda position,

which holds that the present has the future as its *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause) and that the future has the future as its *vipāka-phala* (maturation fruit), because according to them, there exists an *kāraṇa-hetu* in the subsequent associated state (*samanantara-samprayukta*).
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish momentarily.
This claim that all conditioned phenomena perish momentarily differs from the Vātsīputrīyas and others.
Regarding the fact that all dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) have a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), other points are for the most part the same as the tenets of the Dharmaguptaka school.
Regarding those dharmas of the learner (*śaikṣa*) that possess a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), there are two interpretations:

first, that although they are untainted (*anāsrava*) and do not summon tainted fruits, they are nonetheless termed "possessing a ripened fruit" because their preceding [moments] induce subsequent ones as *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruits) and so forth, which mature through transformation;
however, this ripened fruit is in substance actually untainted, for the Sarvāstivādins and others do not admit that what is untainted can be called a "ripened fruit."
Secondly, it is said that one immediately experiences the fruit [of action], as in the case of the first two fruits [of the path].

Just as those who have not yet abandoned desire in the Desire Realm produce Desire Realm fruits through their untainted (anāsrava) karma, so too should one understand the Non-returner (anāgāmin), who produces fruits in the Higher Realms. This is because their afflictions are not yet exhausted and their untainted realization is not yet perfected.
The fundamental tenets of the Sautrāntika school state that the various aggregates (*skandha*) transition from a previous life to a subsequent one;
this is what is designated by the term "transition" (*saṃkrānti*).

The Sautrāntikas assert that while the aggregates transition from a previous life to a subsequent existence as real dharmas, there is no real self (*ātman*) that transitions from the former [to the latter].

Regarding the transition from this world to a future world, if one asks whether this "transition" (vartanā) constitutes permanence, it is because its nature is impermanent; yet, because many [moments] continue to abide, it is called "transition.
Does this apply to internal phenomena (*ādhyātmika-dharma*) or external phenomena (*bāhya-dharma*)?
Apart from the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), there is no eternal cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Apart from the Noble Path, there is no permanent extinction of the aggregates; for the six types of cultivation regarding the outflows cannot sever the afflictions, as they merely suppress them.
There are the aggregates at the limit of the faculties and the single-flavor aggregate.
There is a "root-limit aggregate" (*mūlāntika-skandha*) which is a single-flavored aggregate;

that which is single-flavored has been evolving as a continuous, unified flavor since beginningless time, namely this subtle mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which has never been interrupted. This [consciousness] possesses four aggregates and is called the "root-limit aggregate.

Here, "root" (*mūla*) refers to the aforementioned subtle mental consciousness, which dwells as the very foundation of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); therefore, it is designated as the "root. By means of this...
Because this root gives rise to the five aggregates, it is identical to what is taught by various schools regarding the five aggregates;

however, since the single-flavor aggregate (*ekarasa-skandha*) is the fundamental basis, it is not called a "limit" (*anta*). The remaining interrupted five aggregates are derivative phenomena that arise from it, and are therefore called the "limit-aggregates" (*antaskandha*).
Even during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there exist noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
During the stage of an ordinary person, there also exist noble dharmas, namely the untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*) which are naturally accomplished (*dharmatāpariniṣpanna*).
Their assertion that there exists a person (*pudgala*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) is for the most part similar to the assertions of the Sarvāstivādins.
The adherence to the existence of a person (*pudgala*) as a subtle, ultimately real entity that is difficult to designate— that is, as a true self—

is not the same as the views of the Saṃmitīyas and others, who assert a self that is neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates (*skandha*), but exists as a distinct substance external to them. This is because [the former] maintains that it possesses a distinct essence.
The Tripiṭaka Master, having completed the translation of this treatise, set forth the intent of this re-translation in verse:
Having thoroughly examined the various Sanskrit manuscripts, I have re-translated the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*. Its phrasing is elegant and its meaning is unerring;
The wise should study it with diligence.

The Lokottaravādins maintain that all mundane and supramundane phenomena lack substantial reality and are identical in being mere conventional designations.
The [Lokottara]vādins hold that mundane phenomena arise from perversion, whereas supramundane phenomena possess a distinct and separate essence.
The Kukkutika school:
in ancient times there was a rishi who mated with a hen; the progenitor of this sect was of this lineage.
The Bahulika school.
Having extensively studied the Tripiṭaka and deeply realized the Buddha’s words, they were named the Bahudhātuka (Many-Doctrines) school after their virtue.

The Prajñaptivāda (Proponents of Designation) school asserts that both mundane and supramundane phenomena are all conventionally designated names; because they take these as the ultimate reality, they differ from the aforementioned single school.
The Lokottaravāda school.
Regarding the Caitīya school:
*caitya* is translated as "spiritual shrine" (*lingmiao*). This refers to a mountain where there was a *caitya*, and people lived in reliance upon it; hence the name.
Regarding the names based on mountains:

the Western Mountain Dwelling School (Aparaśaila) and the Northern Mountain Dwelling School (Uttaraśaila) derive their names from the fact that they both resided to the west and north of Mount Caitya, respectively.
The school that propounds causes is also called the Sarvāstivāda (the School of Those Who Assert that All Exists).

"All exists" has two aspects: first, conditioned phenomena exist as real entities throughout the three periods of time; second, unconditioned phenomena exist as real entities apart from the three periods of time.
The name of the school is derived from the principles it establishes.
The Haimavata school was weak and unstable, like snow blown away by the wind; it was named from this simile, and its designation "Haimavata" was established based on its location.
It is also called the Sthavira, a name derived from its distant lineage.
In ancient times, there was a seer of the Vātsīputrīya school who dwelt in a secluded mountain retreat; he became lustful for a mother cow and thereby fathered a son.
From that time on, all of his lineage were named after him.

Regarding "Dharmottara" (Superiority of the Dharma): it refers either to a dharma that can be ascended to, or to a dharma that arises; because many people emerge [therein], it is called Dharmottara, and it is also named after the person.

Regarding the section on "Noble Lineage" (*kṣatriya*): "noble" (*kṣatra*) refers to the head of the clan, while "lineage" (*ya*) signifies offspring; thus, it is by name that these are the offspring of noble arhats.

The Saṃmitīya school weighs and determines that which is called "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*); because it is free from error and delusion, it is termed "correct. This school establishes profound dharmas and meanings;
they are designated by this name because they are seen to be unerring within meditative concentration.
The Mahīśāsaka school is so named because it originated from a place near a mountain forest where the trees were lush and densely thick.
The Mahīśāsaka school.
The founder of this school was formerly a king who converted the earth into a realm of transformation; thus it is called *Mahīśāsaka* (the School of Those Who Abandon the Earth).
Having renounced his kingdom to leave the household life and propagate the Buddha-dharma, he retained his original name.
The Dharmaguptaka school is also known as the Dharmaguptika school.
The meaning of "Sect Master" (bu-zhu) is the same as the meanings of "Treasury" (zang) and "Esoteric" (mi). This master encompasses the True Dharma like a treasury;
thus he is so named. [This refers to] the master Kāśyapa.
In ancient times there was a sage whose body possessed a golden light; because [the Buddha's] golden light obscured that [sage's], he was named Kāśyapa (Drinking Light).
The master of this school is a descendant of him, hence the name. This is the Sautrāntika school.
This school takes only the sūtras as its authority and does not rely on the vinaya or śāstras; thus, it is the Sautrāntika school, which manifests its identity based on what it establishes.
